LADIES' LETTER.

StTv DEAR NELLIIC, Hats for everyday wear are decidedly attractive this season. The indispensible sailor re-appears with a moderately high crown, and a brim a trifle wider than usual. Its trimming, when it is not the plain and manly band, consists of a fold of broad, satin-striped, glacti ribbon round the crown, arid a full, handsome bow in front. Another popu- lar type of useful hat is of Panama straw, aud has a high crown and brim turned up rather deeply at the extreme edge, a bandtau of velvet raising it slightly off the hair at one side. The trimming is composed of a twist of soft bandanna silk round the crown, and a couple of large, loose rosettes of the same placed together with a quill, a little to the aide of the front. Boat-shaped hats of coarse straw trimmed with hackle feather and huge jet buckles suit some faces capitally, while to others the round Spanish shape, with a full bandeau beneath the brim and high-set feather pompons above, proves more becoming.

Lace dresses are rather waning in popularity, or. rather, in fashion, I should say, as they are still pcpular ; but finely-worked Indian muslins and the tambour-worked lawns will be made up into charming summer frocks, with full-flowing skirts, Marie Antoinette fichu, and wide sash ribbons round the waist. The lace coat and the lace bolero, however, continue to play their part in dress, especially with tea-gowns, the latter being worn with Empire frocks and the former with bill-belted gowns of some soft clinging material, over which the lace coat hangs loose and diapha- nous. Einbioideries of flowers in natural colours areAprominent on many pastel-tinted dresses and blouses, but an idea is the use of the peacock's leather, either worked in silks or painted, jewels being w3ecl to accentuate the eye in the middle of each-feather.

Cold winds and bleak skies militate against any great show of spring fashions as yet, which lie lost till a more favourable season arrives. Some wonder iaespressed that greater advantage is not taken of the change of half-mourning, but doubt- less many people, having invested in new black dresses, prefer to finish them out, though a grey gown may be said to be almost as useful as a Ith-• one, and as satisfactory an investment. Grey offers a neutral background for an, additions of colour which afford inits variety in the toilette, and no other tone is quite so good for this purpose. Saud colour and pAtty,sliad yrounse, however, to be the "mbie-Taskuonable this year. Advancing warm weather will see most of the gala frocke_with elbow sleeves and lace ruffles, and with transparent collars, very often with none at all. The ruffle round the shoulders favours the tendency to dc away with the stiff high collar-band, tut here again is a case in which it is better to study one's individual appearance rather than the mode—for the high collar-band is suited to the woman with a long thin neck—and the low neck-bemd should only be worn when the throat is round and white. A
black velvet band is so becoming round the throat that it promises to be well worn, and very pretty clasps and pins for fastening it in front are &feature with many ewel;ers,

This promises to be a great season fo:: outdoor amusements and entertainments, and more atten- tion is being devoted to suitable attire thi.n ever before. For life on the river, or for cycling, the cream oatmeal friezes promise to he greatly worn, and those who really mean work on the water have come to regard serges, friezes, and hornespuns as infinitely preferable to ducks and piqu6s ; the latter are fresh and cool looking, but quickly lose a stiffness and neatness from heat and the splash- ing of sculls and paddles. Nor is a woollen skirt mid blouse any too warm when the wind blows fresh, and they lessen the risk of danger from alas. The sailor hat of the year is narrow in the brim and high in the crown, and the ribbon band irs narrower than of yore. Lengths of silk are now sold ready tucked and veined, all complete for making up Into the popu- lar tucked skirt, which is now so fashionable for morning wear; this removes a great stumbling block to the home-dmssinaker, who wishes to tuck the material after cutting it out, and thereby oiten goes astray in her measurements. Another sew and pretty material for more dressy blouses is oi taffetas, which has stripe of net inserted at in- tervals of two or three inches, on which are 4tplique einbroidern-d medallions, worked in silk ad the mane shade. incrustations of lace ap,soar cfta dal* and evening dresses alike, revealiq a self-tolourn;1 or contrast- ing lining underneath. F.ven with fine faced Moths these lace has:A.o.om are seen. though some- what contrary to one'e idea of the fitness of things. Sprays of ribbon embroidered flowers are much. seen on the fronts of blouses, scalloped under fronts of satin worked with a flower corresponding with the general tone of the blouse being inserted re many of the Dowest models. EZobroidered and brocaded mate will be worn with lace or tambour &arta, in the style of Louis XY. and Louis XVI., kr everykiping tends towards the picturesque in tams this Ileasioa. said, ••I am not married; whatever could nave put such an idea into your bead ?" "But it was stated in the papers that you were married."

"Stated in the papers ? " she questioned, with in- creasing surprise. "Why, yes. It must be three years ago now or more. It was said that you and Phil were married, and had gone on the Continent for your honey- moon."
Ruby rose to her feet, her face very white and her hands trembling. "Did you believe that I had married Phil Passmore ?" she questioned, eagerly. "Why of course we did, Ruby. could we believe ?"
What else
"And did he—that is, did—did—your brother believe it ? "

"I suppose so. Why shouldn't he? We !lune of us had any reason for doubting it. But we did wonder that you never sent us a line." Ruby sat down again, and breathed hard. "Phil Passmore is your cousin," she said at length. "And after—after what had happened I felt I could not write."

"Why ? " Dorothy asked, simply. "Why! Do you not know that he ruined my father. That—that— Oh, I cannot tell you everything." It was now Dorothy's turn to look surprised. "I do not undentand you," she said. "What has Phil done ? We have not heard a whisper about him for years." Ruby clasped and unclasped her hands nervously and her lips trembled, in spite of all her efforts to control herself.

"Father trusted him implicitly, " she said after a long pause, "and then came the crash, and father had to pay everything. I do not under- stand it. Your cousin got quite clear, somehow; not even did his name appear. He professed that he was only a clerk in the firm of Mead, Runcorn and Jago, and somehow those individuals could not be found. Oh, it was an awful time of it. We had to give up our house in Regent's Park and go into a little house in Brondesbury, and then fattier fell ill and in three weeks be was dead--"

"Oh. I did not know," Dorothy said, sympa. thetically. "I am very sorry." "Your cousin never came near us," Ruby went on at length, "but we heard that he blossomed out in greater style than ever and set up an expen- sive establishment in the West End. It did not take long to settle up poor father's affairs, and then mother and I found ourselves almost penni- less. Mother has a little money of her own that grand-father left her, so she decided to go and live with Aunt Jane. But I have nothing; that is the reason I became a nurse."
_ Dorothy drew her chair close up to her friend and kissed her.

"0 Ruby, I am grieved for you," she said. "We had all thought things were so very different. I do not wonder that you did not write to us. But please don't think evil of us because Phil is our relative."

"I do not, Dorothy; please do not imagine that. No, no, it was not that. But when one is 'down, it is not easy to write. You cannot explain things very well, and so you keep silence." "We have often talked about you," Dorothy said at length, "and wondered how you were." "Then you had not quite forgotten me ? " Ruby questioned, with a pathetic smile. "Forgotten you ? Oh, no, Ruby, we were not likely to do that. But you must get some sleep now, for you will need all your strength if you are to pull Justin round. How strange, that of all the nurses in the country the lot should have fallen on you." "Well, you see, I was the only one in the hospital available when the telegram came." "And you knew you were coming here ?" "Not till three minutes before I started. I was told to get ready to go into Cornwall by the next train. The address was given to me when I was ready to start." "It seems a curious chance, or Providence, or whatever you like to call it," Dorothy said, reflectively. "Perhaps in return for saving my life," Ruby answered, "I may be permitted to help in saving his."
"Oh, I hope you will, Ruby. Justin deserves to live. He has worked so hard, and striven so heroically, that it would seem such a mistake and such a waste if he were to die."

Ruby thought so to, but she made no reply, and soon after Dorothy left her. She shut her eyes and tried her best to court sleep, but sleep would not come. Her brain and heart were in a tumult. It seemed so strange that, after all these years, she should come back to nurse the man who had saved her life. The man whose image had been im- pressed on her brain ever since. The one man she had ever cared for. She wondered again if he had cared for her. During the few times he had called upon them in London she had sometimes fancied that the look in his eyes meant more than mere friendship. But in his speech he had been very reticent, and hit manner was almost shy. Now again, in his delirium, he had mentioned her name, and mentioned it in such a way as to make her heart throb wildly. Yet she knew that in such cases people often said the very opposite of what they meant. Hence it was foolish to specu- late on the ravings of a man who was suffering from concussion of the brain. When, two hours later, she went back into Justin's room she found him apparently in a state of coma. The doctor sat by his side with his fingers on his wrist. "He keeps up his strength fairly well," he said, without looking up. "But it will need all our patience and .skill, nurse, to pull him through." "Then perhaps we shall succeed, doctor," she said, with a smile. "You will supply the skill and I will supply the patience." He turned and looked at her with a start. Something in the tones of her voice struck him as being familiar. "Have we met before?" he asked, abruptly. "Then you have forgotten me," she said? looking up at him and smiling. ‘By Jove ! Yes and no. When have we met before ? " "In this house and in this very room. Don't you remember doctoring my sprained ankle ? " "What, arc you Ruby Loveday ? " . "The same." "Of course you are. Good gracious I But-- but--" "Dorothy will tell you all about it," she said, with a smile. "I think we shall succeed now," he said, with a grunt, and he hurried out of the room.

RUBY LOVED AY
BY SILAS K. HOCKING,
Author of "The Strange Adventures of Israel Pendray," "The Day of Recompense," "God's Outcast," "In Spite of Fate," "Her Benny," &c.
CHAPTER XXVII.
IN TEM SHADOW.

"Life is probation, and this earth no goal, But starting-point of man." Justin was found at the bottom of a newly-sunk shaft quite unconscious and apparently dead. How he had got there was by no means clear, and he was able to volunteer no information. It was known that he was anxious to make a thorough inspection of all the "workings "before the general Meeting, and it was supposed that he bad missed his footing, or had been overtaken by faintness, or possibly a stave of the ladder had given way. In any case the result had proved disastrous. Ile lay doubled up in a corner among the rocks. Not a moan escaped his lips, nor could the miners who found him discover the faintest symptom of life. The news of what had happened quickly reached the surface, was carried to Endilloe, and broken gently to Justin's mother. Justin was the very light of her, eyes. Yet she gave no-sign of emotion save that her lips turned suddenly pale. "You say he is -badly hurt ? " she questioned after a long pause, in a dry, hard voice. "Yas, very badly." "Then I must get his room ready at once. He must have the best bedroom, it is the most cheer- ful," and she turned away and mounted the stairs. The doctor was waiting at the mouth of the shaft when Justin was brought to the surface, and a brief examination showed that there was still life in him. But the extent of his injuries would have

to be ascertained later. John and Nathan and Amos came hurrying across the fields with white, haggard faces, and helped to carry Justin home. "He's still living, mother," John said as soon , as they came into the house. "And while 'there's , life, there's hope." Dr. Morrison had already telegraphed to Ply- mouth for a trained nurse who might be expected to arrive some time during the evening. For the next hour a crowd of people waited downstairs. and in the garden for the doctor's 'verdict. conversation tapered out into absolute silence. No one was in the humour for speech. It was all so sad and tragic. Just when toil and effort and patient waiting had brought their reward, this had happened. The luck of the Pentyres had turned, apparently, only to turn again. And yet how little anything mattered. In the presence of death nothing was of any value. Men gained the world and lost their lives. They heaped up treasures for others to gather. Dorothy came downstairs at length with red eyes and trembling lips. "He is living," she said, brokenly, in reply to a dozen inquiries; "and that is about all that can be said. Dr. Morrison says he is terribly hurt. His right leg is broken and his left shoulder dislocated. But that is not the worst. His .head is severely injured, and the doctor is unable to say at present whether it is a case of fractured skull or merely concussion of the brain." "And he is still unconscious ?" someone questioned. "Quite; but he is not in a state of coma. He talks constantly, yet he has not the remotest idea where he is or what has happened to him." So the little crowd dispersed sadly and silently to their homes and to their work, and Dr. Morrison kept anxious watch by Justin's bedside. It was late in the evening and quite dark when the nurse arrived ; a dainty, girlish figure, who ran lightly upstairs and into the sick-room as though she knew the way well. Dr. Morrison met her with a very grave face, and gave her careful and minute instructions which she would have to carry out during the night. "You have had experience in accident cases ? " he questioned. "Yes, a good deal." "You look very young." "I have had three years of hospital work," was the reply. "Ali, that will do. I need not tell you that a good deal will depend upon nursing in this case." "Is it a very bad case ? " "I fear so. But it is impossible to determine just yet the extent of the injuries." "If careful nursing can pull him through," she said, with a little choke in her voice, "then he will get better." When the doctor had left she raised the shade of the lamp a little so that the light fell on the sufferer's face. Then she went close to the bedside and bent over him. Justin lay quite still with closed eyes, but his breathing was heavy and laboured, and his brow was contracted as if he were in pain. The nurse looked at him for a long time without moving, save that once or twice she raised her hand to her eyes as if to wipe away a sudden tear. The sight of this strong, handsome fellow hovering upon the brink of death had evidently touched her sensitive nature. She gave a sigh at length and turned away from the bed and shifted the lamp- shade so that the light no longer fell on Justin's face. Half an hour later Justin's father and mother came into the room, and sat for a long time one on each side of the bed, looking wistfully at the face of their boy, but speaking no word. The nurse, with her face in shadow, watched them intently, but they took very little notice of her. They .stole away at length on tip-toe after a whispered good-night; and for is long time the house was wrapped in a great silence. The nurse drew up her chair near the bed, and watched with curious and sympathetic eagerness every expression that passed over the face of her patient. Soon after midnight Justin opened his eyes and began to talk. At first he appeared to be address- ing a meeting of shareholders, then he began to argue with someone who wanted to steal the farm, and got quite excited over the matter. The nurse rose at once, and laid her hand on his forehead. Instantly he turned his eyes, and looked her straight in the face. "Who are you?" he began; then he paused, and for awhile was silent. "No, no," he went on at length, "you are not old enough or strong enough for our work. Besides, we have taken on all the lianas we can employ on the floors at present--'Count House maid, eh?" hnd he laughed softly. "Well, no. I should have all the neigh- bourhood talking in a week." Then he closed his eyes andlegan to soliloquise. "Pretty girl, that , very pretty girl, reminds me something of Ruby—Ruby—Ruby," and he repeated the name over and over again softly to himself. "They wonder I didn't get married, he said at length, with a smile. "But I never shall. If I hadnever seen Ruby things might have been different. Air I Ruby—Ruby—" and his voice ended in a whisper. The nurse turned and walked to the other end of the room. Such confidences were not for her, and yet she could not help hearing. Justin grew quiet at length, and lay quite still as if asleep. The nurse came back and stood close to his bedside again,- and for the best part of an hour she never once lifted her eyes from his face. The doctor was back again with the dawn, and the household was stirring early. The nurse was ordered to bed as soon as Mrs. Pentyre could take her place. Dorothy came across from her own louse as soon as she could get away. Dorothy and the nurse came face to face on the top of the stairs. The recognition was instan- taneous and complete. "Ruby!" Dorothy cried in astonishment. "Yes, Dorothy," and the next moment they fell to kissing each other, and crying as though these were the only ways open to them of expressing their emotion. Ruby was, the first to recover herself. "Come into my room, Dorothy," she said, "and let us talk; I can't sleep yet if 1 go to bed." Dorothy followed without a word. She was too astonished yet even to ask questions. "You are surprised to see me here," Ruby said, as soon as they were seated opposite one another. "Very much. Ido not understand it at all. Why are yon a nurse ?" "I had to do something for a living," was the seply, "and nursing was the only thing I had a talent for." ' "But—but—what of your husband? Does la elo‘core " "My husband did you say ?—my husband—?" "Yes, you are married, are you not ? " and Dorothy glanced curiously at Ruby's hands, which were perfectly innocent of rings. Ruby gave a little laugh. "No. Dorothy," she

div.head: CHAPTER XXVIIi.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVIIi.
DARKNESS AND DAWN.

"Love heth deep . . . . Love laps his wings on either side the heart." Justin remained in the darkness of mental night for fifteen days. Then after a sleep so long and so profound that the doctor feared he would never wake again, he opened his eyes and looked curiously round him. It was late afternoon, and the room was full of a soft, subdued light. Not a sound broke the stillness except the ticking of a a small clock on the mantelpiece. Ruby sat some distance away, with her face bent over a book. Justin glanced from side to side for several seconds, unable to make out where he was, then he recognised the furniture of the best bedroom, but that scarcely helped him. Why was he in that room at all, and why was lie in bed ? He tried to raise himself on his elbow at length, but fell back, with a low moan. Instantly Ruby dropped her book and came to his side. Her back was towards the window, so that he could scarcely see her face. She saw, however, that he was con scions. and a strange thrill of joy ran through boo "Why am I here, and who are you ? " ii asked, abruptly. "You have been ill," she said, in a whisper. "and I am your nurse. Now, take this and you will feel better."

Be opened his mouth and swallowed the medicine without the faintest protest, but he did not take his eyes from her face for a moment. "Have I been very ill?" he questioned. "I feel curiously weak." "You met with an accident," she said, in the same low whisper, "but you are getting on•nicely." "Ah, yes, I remember. That was this morning. I wonder how I am to get to the meeting ?" "The meeting has been postponed," she answered, "until you are quite well. Now you must keep perfectly still and not worry yourself." He closed his eyes and kept them shut for several minutes. But she saw by his knitted brows that his brain was active. "Would you mind telling me," he said at length, "what day it is ?" "It is Wednesday " she answered, still keeping her voice to a whisper, for she did not want him to recognise her just yet. "Wednesday I" he answered, feebly. "Then I've been off my bead since yesterday."
Yes."

I daresa.v it feels a little stiff and sore, but it will soon be all right again." "And are the T any other breakages ? " he asked, with a pathetic smile. "No, I don't think so. You have only to be patient and obey orders and you'll soon be all right again." "But where is my mother ?" he asked. "She is resting now. She has been with you all the morning, but you were fast asleep." "And have you only just come? " "Dr. Morrison telegraphed to Plymouth as F 00ri ftB it was known you had met with an accident and I was sent off at once."

"Then you are u, regular hospitul nurse „
"Been in the work long ?"

"Three years." And :he turned away and went to the window and drew up the blind and let a little more light into the room. ;Tustin watched her with a wondering expression IA his eyes. He was too weak to think very clearly consecutively, and yet in a hundred ways this tow-voiced nurse reminded him of Ruby. He closed his eyes at length, and tried to live over again some of the old days when hope burnt like a star on the horizon of his life.

Ruby came back to his ,bed again after a few minutes with a glass of jelly and a spoon. "Now you must take this," she said, with a curious little shake in her voice. "If you are to get well quickly, you must take all the nourishment you can." He opened his eyes and looked at her without speaking. She reminded him of Ruby more than ever. They might be twin sisters. "You are very much like a friend of ours," he said, after he had taken two or three spoonfuls of jelly. "Indeed." "I should swear you are the same," he said, 'only, of course, I know you cannot be." Her hand trembled as she passed the scoon again o his lips, but she did not speak. "I never saw two people so much alike," he went on. "It is quite perplexing." "What was your friend's name ? " she asked. "Ruby," he said, faintly. "Ruby Loveday." "My name is Ruby, she answered, in a whisper. He turned his head slightly—he had no strength to do more—and looked at her again. Then their 'yes met in a revealing glance. "Ah !" he said, with a little gasp. "Then lam lot mistaken. You are Ruby, but not Ruby Loveday." "Yes, I am Ruby Loveday," she answered, with a pathetic smile. "No; please do not talk any more now. lam afraid you have already talked too much. When you are stronger you shall know s.ll you want to know." "No, no," he whispered, pleadingly. now. I shall worry if you don't." "Then close your eyes and keep very still. rhere is not very much to be told. Father trusted your cousin, Mr. Passmore, and lost everything. I think it broke his heart. He died three years Igo. So mother went to live with her sister, and I have earned my living ever since as a nurse. How the report got about that I was married, I do not know. It is utterly false. I would sooner have died any time than married Phil Passmore. Now you know everything. Don't ask any more ques- tions now, but get some sleep if you can." He opened his eyes and smiled at her, then with s whispered "thank you," closed them again, and soon after he seemed to be fast asleep.
"Tell me

A week later, not only Ruby, but the doctor had nearly given up hope. Justin had recovered con- sciousness and gladdened the hearts of his father and mother and Dorothy by recognisins.' them again, but he did not recover strength. Day by day he grew weaker, and it seemed as if nothing Dn earth could save him. He lay quite still with- out a moan and without ever a word of regret. Now and then he smiled at his mother and the rest, but he was too weak to talk, or the effort seemed too great for him to make. It was nearly an hour past midnight, and Ruby was watching by his side. She was nearly heart- broken. She had hoped that she might repay him for saving her life by helping to save his, but it seemed as if it were not to be. If ever nursing was a labour of love, it was so in her case. She had cherished his memory for years. All the romance of her life had gathered round his name. From the day he had plucked her out of the hands of the cruel sea, and had carried her home through the moonlight in his strong arms, and she had felt his cheek close to hers—there had been no other in the world that could compare with him. His very reticence and apparent coldness seemed but to increase her love for him. He was so different from the shallow, flippant youths who gathered round her and paid her silly compliments. He was strong and reliant, and a man to be trusted. He feared God and reverenced his parents, and was ss devoted as a lover te his sister. Such a man was worth knowing and worth loving. And yet she did not dream of love at first. She admired him and reverenced him. But out of reverence, love grew little by little. She found herself dreaming about him and hoping she would meet him. And when disaster overtook her father, she almost pined for a sight of his face, for she :elt sure they would have his sympathy. Then followed silent years of toil, and when she came as far west as Plymouth, she wondered if they would ever meet again. Justin was her ideal still —the one man she could ever love. Was it Providence that she should have been sent to nurse him? She almost thought so at first. God was good to her, and was going to allow her to pay a debt that long had lain upon her heart. But now as she sat watching him in the solemn bush of the night, it almost seemed as though Prcr7idence were mocking her. They had met but to part again for ever. "Ruby!" The word fell faint upon her ear as the sighing of a zephyr. "Will you come a little nearer. I want to talk to you." She gulped down a sob that had risen in her throat, and was by his side in a moment. "I think I shall not get better," he went on, faintly. "I seem to be slipping out of life." "No, no, don't say that," she answered; chok- ingly. "You must not give up hope." "I have tried not, but—but—well, it cannot be helped," he whispered, faintly, "but I want to tell you something before I go." She bent over him with eyes brim full of tears, out did not answer him. "Perhaps I ought to be thinking of other things," he went on, "but I cannot help telling you, Ruby. I have loved you ever since that night I found you 3n the beach. Loved you! Ah ! none but God san tell how much I have loved you. I went to London that I might be near you, and in spite of 3ircumstances I clung to the hope that I might win you. What I suffered during that fruitless struggle no one will ever know. Then I missed you and found your house empty, and it was rumoured that you were married. So I turned my back upon London, which I had endured only because of my love for you. It was sweet to come home again, and for years I have worked, glad that I had loved even though I had lost. "It was strange that you should find me here. I think it was God who sent you. And for weeks on have nursed me with patient kindness. And I rave not minded the suffering since you were near me. I hope you do not think I do wrong in telling you this, Ruby. No harm can come of your know- ing that I have loved you and that I love you still. "I know I was never worthy of you, Ruby, but that does not matter now— Suddenly she lifted her face, while the tears streamed down her cheeks. "Hush I hush !" she cried. "You must never say that again or even think it. Not worthy of me. 0 Justin—" and she dropped on her knees and buried her face in the bedclothes. For awhile the silence was broken only by Ruby's sobs. Then Justin spoke again in the faintest whisper: 'Don't. cry," he said, "I did not mean to assa you. !I won't cry if you will get better," she said, smiling at him through her tears. "If you love me you must get well again for my sake." He reached out his wasted hand to her and she took it in both of hers and kissed it. Then he understood, and soon after he fell asleep again. For another twenty-four hours his life trembled in the balance. ;Ruby, Dorothy, and his mother watched by him with infinite solicitude and with unfailing patience and love, and when at length the tide of life that had ebbed out so far began to flow back again, old Dr. Morrison rubbed his hands and declared that it was the nursing that had done it.

summer was quite over when Justin was able to get downstairs again. But Nature is generous in that western county, and there were lovely autumnal days when the sun shone out of a cloud- less sky and not a leaf stirred on the trees, when the flowers still bloomed in the garden, and the air was like nectar.

Ruby would remind Justin of the days when she was the invalid and he was her good and gallant knight, and he would look at her and smile, fox' speech was too clumsy a medium to reveal what was in his heart.

Those were happy days for both. Before the days of fog and rain came on, he was able to get as far as the cliffs and listen again to the deep music of the sea. All restraint had long since dis- appeared, and they talked as lovers should. Ruby did not go back again to Plymouth, but she went on a long visit to Dorothy and helped her to nurse her first-born. During the spring a new wing was added to Endilloe, and then the people , of St. lago began to talk and to put two and two together and to prophesy. Nathan was still convinced of the general igno- rance of town's people, but he admitted that Ruby was an exception. "She's what I call a beauty," he said to Amos. "A purtier, or a sweeter, or a brighter little maid I've never seed, an' if I'd been forty year younger I should ha' tumbled in love-with her myself." Early in March Amos got his heart's desire and more. His son Dan'l came home for a visit, bring- ing his bride with him, a happy, good-looking, light-hearted lass, who turned all her a's into i, and all her r's into w's, and who went into raptures over everything she saw. Amos laughed till the tears ran down his face, and when Dan'l's wife kissed him he blushed till his face was scarlet.
Nathan received quite a shock when he saw Dan'l. The freckled, loutish youth had become a smart, well-dressed man, who evidently had all his wits about him. _ _ .
"I'm not goin' to say, Amos," he said, "that your Dan'l ain't terribly improved, but then you know he growed up in the country, and that makes oal the difference.

"But look at his wife," said Amos. in triumph. "An' she was born up there in that big town." But Nathan vouchsafed no answer; the problem was beyond him. Had a stranger been passing through St. lege one morning early in May he would have discovered that something unusual had happened, or was happening. The whole place had quite a festive appearance. Bunting was flying from the engine- houses and from the top of the "Shears," and from stump frames, and from the counting-house windows. The village-street was thronged with boys and girls. The Methodist Chapel was crowded to its utmost capacity, while so many carriages with grey horses attached had never been seen in St. lago before. Justin was still pale, and walked with just perceptible limp when he left the chapel with his happy young bride leaning on his arm. Ruby looked younger and lovelier than ever. . _

Over the 17reakfast-table there was a good deal of speech-making, and when Justin, in reply to the toast "The health of the bride and bridegroom," said "I went away to seek my fortune, and came home to find it," there was a burst of cheering that could be heard to the end of the garden. Some thought of the fortune in Wheal Patience Mine, and some thought of Ruby. But those who were watching Justin closely and saw the look in his eyes as he glanced towards his beautiful young wife, knew well enough what was in his heart. He did not despise the _rich acres of Endilloe,
nor the wealth in Wheal Patience Mine, but Bub, was more to him than everything else on earth. [TEE END.]

-- The King is spending Eastertide at Windsor with his grandchildren, the little Princes and Princess of York. It was not until His Majesty promised that the little folks should be expressly looked after by himself and by the Queen, that the Duchess of Cornwall and York was satisfied to leave her children for seven or eight months. That they are most tenderly cared for goes with saying. Wherever they are, there is always a physician stayine under the same rcof, who sees the Royal children every day. There are also three curses and a governess, and those in charge of the little Princes usually find them- selves pretty well occupied, as Prince Edward and his brothers are full of boyish spirits and up to all sorts of daring exploits. Prince and Princess Charles of Denmark, who have been staying over here for several months, will spend the iemainder of the spring at Mentone. Though the King's youngest daughter is devoted to outdoor exercise, she is not very strong, and being subject to neuralgia, she prefers to spend the season in the south of Europe. Her Royal Highness is very fond of yachting, and she can find many opportunities for indulging in this recrea- tion on the Mediterranean. She is also a fine horse- woman, and a keen cyclist. These are her favourite diversions, but Princess Maud, as she is sometimes called, is a clever photographer, a good chess player, and is net only familiar with several languages, but like all the King's daughters, she possesses many cicmeszic accomp- lishments. There are rumours suggesting the engagement of Princess Margaret of Connaught to the Crown Prince of Germany. The Duchess of Connaught as the daughter of the Red Prince is popular in Germany, but it may be taken for granted that the Kaiser has other ends in view for his eldest son. In the first plac.., early marriages are not encouraged in Germany, and there is little doubt that a political alliance will be sought for the Crown Prince. If, as many think, Austria is eestined to be absorbed ty Germany, it is probably in that direction that the Crown Prince will look for his Consort. Proba- bilities would therefore point to his alliance witn this Archduchess Elizabeth, the Austrian Emperor's grand- daughter, who, but for the operation of the Salle Law, would be heiress to the Austrian Throne. The only obstacle would be one of religion,but Austrian Princesses have before now adopted Protestantism in order Co

marry Prussians. Lenten weddings are not so infrequent as in f lrmer years, still, to a great many people this season is strictly barred from choice, and so also is May, on account of the ill-luck that is proverbially associated with that month. "Marry in May, and rue for aye," is a tradi- tion which is still very much believed in by marrying folk, and there will consequently be a great pressure of weddings during the present month. One item, in the matter of marriage and giving in marriage, to be de- I plored, la the donning of jewels by up to-date brides. For some time past,ornaments have—for such occasions —been deemed unnecessary and in doubtful taste and one can but regret their return to favour. The numerous jewels worn just now give an overdressed theatrical air to the best dressed bride. For quiet wed- dings, one bridesmaid—or to use the new title" maid of bonour"—only, is considered correct. Invariably she is garbed in white, thereby forming a delightful foil to the bride who in such instances usually elects to wear a touch of colour. I Like many old threatened institutions, the hot-cross bun still survives. It has long been supposed to be in a bad way, so much so that when the associated bakers recently considered the proposal to abolish the Good Friday bun, it was announced that they had unani- mously decided to have no more of it. The trade they said, has been gradually declining year by year, but in spite of all these complaints and protests, buns seem to be as plentiful as ever this Eastertide. That is to Fay in those districts—the Southern and Midland counties— where it is most favoured. The hot-cross bun is never seen on the Continent, and it is but little Known in this country in the North, BO that it can hardly be said to be a national institution. Lady Jenne who is a keen observer of social habits and customs, regards excessive tea-drinking as a great thief of vitality. To the undue resort to the teapot, she attri- butes the delicate appearance, the colourless cheek, and the languid eye of so many girls of the working class, especially amongst those in domestic service. Tea is nearly always handy, and whatever its virtues, it usually causes indigestion, and thus prevents the proper nourishment of the body. Then again, multitudes of young women who no longer look to a sheltered home life, but go out to business to earn their own living, often pay too little regard to their food requirements. Any light meal, they have been accustomed to remark, will do for them. but, as a matter of fact, such make- shifts are not sufficient for the wear and tear of an arduous business life. We know that taken as • whole the people of the present day live better, live longer and more healthy lives than formerly, but at the same time Lady Jenne is perfectly justified in warning us against the abuse of the tea-pot, and the neglect of dieting as two of the common failings of our sex. The straight-fronted corset is steadily gaining ground and leading moiistes show a decided objection to fit one over any other style. There can be no possible question concerning the desirability of the straight-fronted variety. It is undeniably a most rational style, it is much more cemfortable to wear, and gives a smaller effect than the old cut of Corset. Concerning waistbands on all the smartest gowns, these are well pulled down in front. This mode which is much patronised by the Queen, and the Duchess of Cornwall and York, is be- coming to slim and stout alike, giving a long, slender- waisted appearance to the wearer. The sailor hat, though no longer popular with the ex- clusive ones, will still find favour among less exalted folk, for morning, and later on for seaside and country wear. The shape of the year is high in the crown, and narrow in the brim, and the ribbon band will not be more than an inch wide. The bike capeline promises to enjey a wide vogue egain this coming summer. The best have a double frill of lace, wired and undulated, to look like the petals of a flower. Worn above a fresh young face ihe capeline is unquestionably one of the most fascinating styles of headgear we have ever seen, but, it should be remembered that only the quite young can done it to advantage. Ludicrous indeed appeared some of the would-be youthful wearers of the cspeline last year. Let us hope that such exhibitions will be epaied us during the season to come. Lovely blouses, or. " corsages " are being made of wide dike ribbon, and lace insertion, the jolt s teeing hidden under a species of feather stitch, or cross stitch. Chine ribbons are enjoying a wide vogue both for the purpose named. and In the miltiaery world. Some have quite a distinct pattern, others—the most approved— have an indefinite pattern of blurred, rich tints. The Exhibition, and Sale of Iriah industries has greatly stimulated the use of lace,which will be extensively used by both milliners and dressmakers during the late Spring and summer months. Stuffed Eggs.—Cut some bard-boiled eggs in halves, mix each yolk with a teaspoonful of grated cheese, and a small piece of butter. Season with salt,cayetine,and a grating of nutmeg. Refill the whites, and serve on a bed of cress.

div.head: TALE OF THE AMERICAN CIVIL WAR
div.p: TALE OF THE AMERICAN CIVIL WAR
/IT MAJOR T. PRESTON BATTERSBY, ,Author of "My Swim to the Target," "A Question
of Expediency," &c.

'Ti the spring of the year 1837 I chanced to be in London on professional business, and to have a clay at my own disposal. I had been read- ing Mr. Besant's famous novel, "All Sorts and Conditions of Men," and it struck me that I could lake no better use of my time than to employ some of it in a tour through the wonderful East End of London, so vividly pourtrayed by the author. With this end in view, I dressed myself in an unpreten- ti, ous shooting costume which had done much service ln the Irish bogs, and started on my explorations. I certainly saw a good deal that was new to me in the East End—much that was saddening, much that was hopeful. Towards midday, feeling the need of some refreshment, I strolled into a tavern in the Lhnehouse direction (I forget the name of the street, if indeed I ever knew it). There were not 1131, anY People there, no doubt because it was the .rasy time of the day; only one or two dock labourers out of work, and a handsome bearded tom in a sailor's dress. They were enjoying pipes Lind beer at a table some way removed from the and I took my seat at another, within hearing distance, and called for a mug of ale. I hoped to hear something of the ways of the people of the Place in listening to my neighbours' conversation. To my great disappointment, I found that they Were merely discussing that most wearisome of all lubjects, the Irish land question. I could hear sal that was to be said on that matter in the West lid any day, so I determined to drink my beer as Last as possible and move on in search of more interesting scenes. But it was fated otherwise. My neighbour of 'he beard, who had apparently not joined in the conversation, smote his hand upon the table with a force which made the glasses ring, and gave utterance to his opinion as follows: 'You chaps may talk as much as you please, and Inay old Gladstone, and Salisbury, and all the Nt of them. But mark my words—none of you ;1111 ever make anything of those infernal Irish! th eY are that 'cute that there is no being up to eir tricks I ought to know it, if any man eh° ud' and if that gent (nodding at me) cares to _ear a good story, and to stand drinks round, I Z 414 promise to tell him something he never heard ,"gore. Maybe, sir, you are one of those chaps that writes for the papers; and if you are, I can 'tell you you might lay out your money worse." I owned to the soft impeachment of being "a chap that writes," and expressed my readiness to stand drinks not once, but twice, should the story promise well. Matters being thus amicably settled, and myself unanimously elected to a seat at the table, my friend took a mighty pull at his pot of ale, and thus began: "It was in the year '64, lads, that what I am going to tell you happened. I was out in America When the great war began, and pretty hard up, too, so I thought I couldn't do better than ship on board a Federal man-o'-war, and see a little aghting. Those were fine times for us sailors, for the Government turned out ships faster than seamen—who were scarce in the market—could be found to man them. I saw fighting enough to last roe all my life, I can tell you; and if I had time . l° spare, I would spin you a yarn that would last „lrem this till to-morrow. I was on board of the V-oosatonic, off Charleston, when the Confederates .1 • clew her up, and, you bet, I don't want to be blown up again. D—n those torpedoes I say I. There was an end to all fair fighting when they Were invented." "What's a torpedo, master ? " asked one of the _°lll pan y. "I never mind that I heered the word uefore." _

„ Lucky for you, then, my son! ” said the sailor. only wish the Confederates had never heard, I'll tell you how we lost the Hoosatonic, 144 d then you'll be a wiser man. The rebels had i!tdiving boat at Charleston, which some clever -`l4ll, invented before the war began. It moved 11:ger the water, and the crew got air through a n„lat indiarubber tube with the end fastened to a v;at• They worked her with handles inside, which turned by the crew, and moved paddle-wheels i! Some sort. She must have been a slow moving of a craft at the best. The first time they ,dried her she turned turtle, and drowned all her been but the lieutenant in charge. He must have peen a chap of good grit, for when, we were blockading Charleston in '63 nothing would suit him but to rig up a pole at her bows, with a big charge of powder at the end, and go out to try his luck on the Federal fleet.

"He had a crew of fellows as desperate as him- 'Self, and I'm blest if they didn't run their cockle- shell slap into the stern of the old Hoosatonic! Off went the powder, and down, went we, with a hole in our timbers as big as a church door! I heard afterwards-that the boat went down too, for aue had too much way on, and couldn't reverse her engine in time, so she ran straight into the hole she had made, and foundered along with the ship. I was on deck at the time when it happened, and had just sense enough left to jump into the water with a life buoy, and so got off safe. But many a Vod fellow was drowned that day." He took a look at his listeners, and, evidently pleased by the awestruck expression of their 'rnountenances, continued his story, in which I was aow greatly interested, as I knew that so far his facts were certainly true enough. "In December, '64," he went on, "I was second mate on board of a gunboat, and, with eight Others, we were sent up the Roanoke River to burn the railway bridges at VVelden. The rebel General tee was drawing his supplies by that line of rail, and we wanted to starve him out. We got up the river about forty miles very comfortably, and then the fun began. Those knowing chaps had sown the river with detonating torpedoes, that went off When a ship's keel touched them. We sent out our boots, with nets and grapnels, and they Managed to find a good many of the infernal things, but, there were enoligli left to do the mischief. In one day four of our vnboats were sent to the bottom, and three others so damaged that we could scarcely keep them afloat. We turned tail then, and made off down the river, expecting every lmoment to hear another explosion, and see another ahip go down. However, we managed to get back 811 right; but when we neared the mouth of the river one of the damaged boats Nits found so leaky that the officer in command of the expedition ordered the captain of my vessel, which was one of the two uninjured, to steam off down the river till found a spot where it would be possible to lay • gunboat on the mud at low water and get at 0 hole in her bottom from the outside. Having t;lald a suitable place, he was to leave buoys to it, and then make the best of his way to the CWlron at sea, and report what had happened to erpedition. a.hl.'-'man tell you none of us were sorry to have a allee of leaving that cursed river, and you may be ▪ to that we hurried as much as possible to coin- ate our work. But it was not until we got into „we estuary that we found just such a spot as we 'equired. There was a strongish tide running, so 13ve anchored our vessel, and prepared to put out We were not more than three-quarters of a mile from the shore; and we had not been ten tainutes at anchor before we saw a little cockleshell Of a boat, with one man in her, pulling out towards 14' None of us could imagine what he was up to, uut when he got within hailing distance the captain !thnuted to him to keep off, and tell his business Where he was. You see, after that Hoosatonic affair and our losses in the river, none of us knew What those fellows might undertake, and it was as Well to be on the safe side. "The chap in the boat pulled in his oars as ~9olly as may be, and pitched out a stone with a !Inn fastened to it from the bow of his craft, as an Then he sat down in the stern sheets, and Lbegan lighting his pipe, with all the ease in life, wiLile we all waited to hear what he had to say. t, What in thunder do you want here? ' shouts, hue captain at last; and we knew by his voice that is getting a trifle riled. 0 Li' -the fellow grinned, and the moment he opened 1, mouth we knew him for an Irishman • Ye needn't be so oncivil, captain, he says, When I've conie all this way to have the pleasure tin .discoorsin' with yer honour. Sure, it's on _lanaaa I'm here, and glad I'll be to have a con- too:ttion with a gentleman like yerself. You know that me name is Pat Maguire, and .001,orother's name is Tins, and we come of the Iserrn' Mapires that were Kings in the county T,lagn, and sn____' you and your brother, and the shouts the captain. Will you tell Ak_ Your business, or must I Bend a round shot -.vouch your boat to teach von manners?

div.p: Diusha, then, maybe the teaching will be the other way! ' says the Irishman. But if ye will have it, sure it's not for the likes of me to prevent ye. I came out to tell yes all that yer ship hi anchored over the foinest torpedo ever yes seen, and me brother Tim is on the shore beyont there with the electric battery; and if ye make the haste or to move yer boat, up she goes, and the Lora have mercy on yer souls is the prayer of Pat Ma„euire ! ' "The captain looked at the first mate, and he looked at me, and the crew looked at us three. We were none of us cowards, but I don't think there was a man on board who hadn't 4 white face just then. Remember, it was not three days since we had seen what torpedoes could do, and now we were in a fair way to feel it. "The captain leant over the side, and spoke to the chap in the boat in a very different tone from that which he had used a minute before. He had given a nod to the mate first, and that officer was making a survey of the shore with a telescope to see what truth there was in the story. "‘ Well, Pat,' says the captain where was the use of your coming out here? Why don't you blow us up and have done with it ? ' "‘ Sure, captain,' the Irishman, it was that same we were going to do; but me and Tim talked it over, and we thought after all there might be some good Catholics aboard of you, and even if there weren't there might be some of you who would turn some day, if you were let live long enough. So Tim say "Pat," says he, "take the coracle, and pull out to them, and see if ye can't make a small matter of an agreement with them, for sure they can't but be grateful to ye for saving their lives, and it wouldn't be much for gintlemen like them to make up two thousand dollars among them. With that we might go home to the oult country, and take a lease of Owen Ikrady's fa XI, and have it to say all our lives that we had saved a good fifty persons from death in the great war." "Tim," says I, "you're right, and yer words are the words of a good Christian." So now, captain dear, I'll give ye five minutes to think it over; only don't be going to move the ship, or Tim will have ye all in the air, by the holy poker ! ' "At this juncture the mate touched the captain on the arm, and informed him that there could be no doubt that the story was true, for he could distinctly see a man sitting on the shore under a projecting rock, and watching the ship with a field- glass, while beside him stood an electric battery, of which he could even see the firing key. "‘ A round shot might reach him, he said; but supposing we missed! ' "‘ Nonsense ! ' said the captain, turning round; there is not • gunner on board who could hit so small a target at that distance, and he would have time to blow us up, when he saw the flash, before a shot reached him. Now, men, what is to be done? You are all concerned, and shall have • voice in the matter.' "Everyone was for consenting to the demand. I suggested that it might be possible to decoy the Irishman on board the ship, and then steam away with him, as his brother would scarcely blow him up with us. The captain, however, shook his head. We can try,' he said, but I doubt he will be too many for us.' Then, leaning Over the gunwale, he addressed our persecutor, in a voice as soft as a lady's. Pat,' said he, I'm afraid we haven't as much as two thousand dollars in cash on board the boat, and I suppose you won't take paper; but if you will come on board here, we will see what we can muster amongst us.' "‘ Very well, captain, answered the Irishman. ' But yell give me yer word of honour not to play any tricks, or move yer ship while I'm aboard of her. It wouldn't save ye if ye did, for Tim's a terrible fellow; but I wouldn't like to lose me own life, so ye must swear to me not to betray me. ' "The captain made the promise most unwillingly. Pat leisurely lifted his killick, and came on board, and we all mustered on the quarterdeck. The captain made us a speech, and sent us below to fetch up what money lye had. "As for me, I had been playing cards the night before, and luck was against me, so all I had left was one dollar. I was none the less angry for that, you may be sure. I shook the coin out on the table in the cabin. My bowie knife was lying there, a splendid bit of steel, which I have still ; and the thought came to me to put an indelible mark on my Not that I'm likely ever to see it or l'ise Maguire again,' I said to myself. But, at all events, the villain will have some trouble in passing it.' . .

"I took my knife out of the sheath, and with a good blow struck its point right through the coin. I had done the same before with ten-cent pieces, which are harder. Twice I pierced the dollar, to make sure that I could know it again, and then I went on deck, where we each laid down our money in a heap, and the captain took a note of the sums. _

"I do not think any of us kept back anything; but money was scarce in those days, and, when every coin on board was in the heap, the captain had only registered one thousand two hundred dollars. " You must take this, Pat,' said the captain gravely; you see it is all we can make up amongst us. "‘ Well, sir, to oblige you, I will,' answered our persecutor. But Tim and me must have s real gould watch apiece to tell the time of day by when we get back to the ould country; and neither cif us are over well fitted out. A dozen of shirts, now, and a suit or two of clothes, won't be too much to ask of jou, seeing we're after saving all yer lives.' "It was a hard pill to swallow, but thero was no help for it. Pat pocketed the gold watches of the captain and first mate, provided himself with a bundle of linen and clothes selected from the wardrobes of the officers, had his money put in a sack, and carefully lowered into the boat, and then made his last request—or rather, gave his last order. •

- "'There's only one thing more now, captain and gentlemen all. Ye wouldn't hear me tell ye the histhory of the ould Maguires of Permanagh just now, and ye insulthed their memory, so with yet good leaves we'll have a jar of whisky on deck, and drink to the health of, all the ould.fanzilies in Ireland, and the Maguires in particular, and then I'll say good evening to yez. , "We did it, .1 am ashamed to say—actually drank Pat's toast to his dictation, and shook bands meekly with him all round. He bestowed his blessing upon us, and departed, after swearing over the captain to give him half an hour's law from the time his boat touched the shore. The instant he landed, he and his brother could be seen with the telescope to bring out a cart from behind a rock, load it with their plunder, and drive away at a quick trot, abandoning their battery. When the half-hour had expired a strong party of us went on shore to cut the wires. We found none. What we had taken for a galvanic battery was nothing in the world but an old wooden biscuit-box with two empty whiskey jars standing in it, and a brass door- knob stuck on tlos And it was for that rubbish that we had just paid one thousaad two hundred dollars!"

Here the narrator paused, and was greeted by a general roar of laughter, which at first seemed to annoy him, but in which he soon joined himself. "Is that ?" I asked, seeing a look in his eye which led me to surmise that he had more to tell. "Not quite," he answered, "and as I have, told eo much I may as well tell the rest, though I am not proud of it. "You bet, after the captain knew how he had teen bamboozled he was determined to keep the affair a secret. When we reached the squadron he paid each of us what we had lost, with something over, and asked us, as a favour, that none of us would disclose what had happened. We weren't so proud of it as to be eager to let the sailors of the fleet hear of our proceedings, and, so far as I-can tell, the secret, did not leak out till years after. There were five of us on board who were Englishmen, and we all refused the captain's money, and vowed that we would keep Pat Maguire in our debt until we could pay him in full. "Whenever we got access to any of the rebel prisoners we made a point of asking after the two Maguires,but never a word could we hear. No one seemed to know them. When the war was over, and we w.re our own masters again, I just took a tour, with one or two more, through the villages near the Roanoke. At last l came on traces of our friend in a place they call Plymouth, on the south shore of Albemarle Sound, not very far from where we had been made such fools of. There I met a man who knew the Maguires well. Tim, he said, had been killed in a fight, after he bad been drunk for a fortnight (with our money, no doubt); Pat had disappeared after his brother's death, and was supposed to have embarked for Europe. "4 They were a queer couple, said my in- formant; they were so poor when they came to Plymouth that they had to beg a drink; and when Tim died his pockets were full of dollars. No one knew how they came tiy it. I remember asking Pat one day, and he shewed toe a dollar he bad

with a note dug througu it. tie Amu hung it on his geld watch-chain, and said it brought him luck. I heli e myself he stole it, and the watch too. Maybe lou know something of it, as you are asking about hits ? ' He looked at me curiously. "` How should I?' asked I, • when I was a sailor on board ship at the time you talk of.' I had no idea of letting the Plymouth folks crow over me, whatever the Irishmen might do. "Well, to make a long story short, neither I nor my comrades could trace Pat Maguire any f either, in spite of the clue we had to him through his wearing my marked dollar. And when our money ran out, which was very soon, we all shipped on board different vessels, bound for different parts of the world, and I have never seen any of them since. "As for me, I got a berth on board a trader, and last year we put into Cork harbour. It was close on Christmas-time, and I thought I would go on shore and have a spree in honour of the season. The mate went with me, and we hired a couple of horses and rode out to some village in the mountains, whose name I can't remember, and couldn't pronounce if I did. We each had a whisky flask, and by the time we got to the village we were not quite as sober as we might have been. There was some Nationalist demonstration going on, and the first thing we met was a procession of men on horseback, in green coats and with the horses' manes and tails tied up with green ribbons. They had a big flag with them, and when he saw it the mate says to me : Jim, yonder's a pirate flag; let's capture it! " Agreed,' says I; and we kicked our horses into a gallop, and cheered for the Queen. Next thing I remember I was lying in the road, with half a dozen fellows kicking at me and hammering me with their fiats and a noise like Bedlam broke loose going on all round. I thought I was done for, when up rides a man on a tine horse, and jumps off close by. What's all this ? ' says he. The green chaps all shouted at once, and the man blew a whistle, and presently a lot of police came running up, and my assailants stopped beating me, and most of them ran away. Give me your hand, and I will help you up, says the gentleman to me. I hope you are not much hurt? " I'm all right, sir, barring a few bruises,' said I; but when I came to risel found I was stiffer than I thought, and I only saved myself from falling by catching hold of the man's coat. He was a strongly-built chap, and only staggered a little; but the coat buttons flew, and I just slipped gently down again on the ground, with a piece of cloth in my hand, and something else too, that had been torn from his watch-chain, I suppose. You mayn't believe me, mates, but as sure as I ,it here it was my own marked dollar I I should have known it anywhere. "You bet, it was not long till I was on my feet again, sore as I was, and looking lido the gentle- man's face. He wore a heavy moustache, and only for the dollar I should never have known him, but since I had seen that I had no doubt. He was dressed in a good suit of broadcloth, and looked every inch the gentleman. Ohl you thundering villain!' I shouted, and went for him straight. But two policemen collared me before I could touch him. He came forward and looked me full in the face; but he didn't recognise me till I said something about torpedoes and the Roanoke River. Then he saw he had lost his dollar, and took in the situation at once. Let him go, policemen,' he said, laughing. 'Why, this is one of the hundred and fifty men whose lives I saved in the American war! ' and with that he gave me a wink to hold my tongue. I knew I could not fight him, and the policemen at once, so I did not say a word. • Come with me! ' says he.' We must have a talk over old times together.' I followed him, thinking I might get a chance of a fair stand up fight; but he opened the breast of his coat again when we had got a little way from the police and shewed me the butt of a revolver. • Now,' says he, • I gave you your chance before in the Roanoke River, and now I will give it to you again. Will you come home and dine with me like a Christian, and promise to forget everything that happened on the other side of the Atlantic, or shall I have you arrested by the police as a dangerous character, and give you three months in gaol? For I am a magistrate now, you must know —Patrick Maguire, Esquire, J. P., at your ser- vice! ' "I didn't know what to do, and I stood there thinking, and he laughed at me, with his hand on his revolver, for fear I might make a spring at him. At last I said: Well, Mr. Patrick Maguire, if your biscuit-box on the Roanoke was worth two hundred and forty pounds, the story I might tell of it here is worth as much to yea now, you must allow.' " 'Not a farthing!' says he. 'Who would believe you? 1. am the most popular man in the county now, and do you think, they would take your word against mine? And if they did, what then? All's fair in love and war, and there isn't a man in the country who would not think the trick I played you as good a joke as ever they heard. But I don't want to be hard on you, and if you'll shake hands, and let bygones be bygones, I don't mind paying you back your share of the contribution, and giving you something in addition to remember me by. Is it a bargain ? ' 4i4 All you got from me was that marked dollar, said I. Give me that back ' (for one of the policemen had taken it from me and given it to Maguire), and I'll cry quits with you as far as I am concerned. But if any of my comrades ever asks me to help him to pay you out on his own score, I will., You see, I was a trifle angry by this time at the coolness of the scamp. "I can't give you that,' said he. It has brought me luck, and I mean to stick to it. But I will buy it of you for a sovereign, and leave you your full rights of revenge in the future if you like. Come now, and have dinner!' "He looked so jolly and cheerful that I couldn't bear malice any longer, so I followed him to his house—a right fine one it was, too. He gave me a good dinner, and a skinful of whisky—the best I ever tasted—and when I went away he gave me the sovereign he had promised me, and what no called a keepsake to remember him by—the captain's gold watch and chain. "The mate had fled for his life before the greencoats, and managed to get off scot-free. I read him a lesson on his cowardice when I got back, you may be sure. I have never seen Mr. Patrick Maguire attain, or any of my Roanoke comrades; but as ''for the captain's watch, here it is!" With that the sailor pulled a gold watch from his pocket, and handed it round for inspection. "Seems to me, mate, you did not make a bad thing out of the business after all I" remarked one of the men. "Not in money," said the sailor. "But still, I was done by an Irtsliman, and that goes against the grain. But I may be even with him yet, for all his Esquire and J.P." I thanked him for his narrative, and paid for another set of drinks, and then we parted, mute. ally pleased with our afternoon's entertainment in the East End. _

Satisfactory Result. The Wesley an body at Padgate is making an effort to extaugaise a debt on the church and, ale° to form tne nucleus of a fuod for a further exten- sion at an early date. It was considered that the most desirable way of accomplishing the end in view was to inaugurate a bszaar cud the ladies and friends of the congregcion have been busily en- gaged for several cnonats in preparing articles for sale. The "Violet Blzaar " was the aurae'lee title given to the venture, 'led for the opening day on Thursday afternoon last week, the promoters were fortunate in securing Mrs J Caarlton Parr to per- form the opening ceremony. The little school- room was utilized to toe beet advantage and looked exceedingly pretty with its attractive stalls, artistically draped in violet material of var- ious shades. Violet was the distinguishing colour everywhere. The delicate little lower which bears the name was freely worn and was also used in the decoration of the stalls, whilst the young ladies in charge of them wore sashes or ribbon of the same hue. Tae accommodation was too limited to eliow of any entertainments in the echoolroom, bat this difficulty was surmounted by the erection of a special annexe, The work had been entrusted to Messrs Wilkinson, Martin and Co. of Liverpool and a well-lighted and commodious annexe with a raised platform at the end was pro- vided. In addition to the entertainments the annexe was also used for refreshment purposes. The stalls contained a choice collection of plain and fancy needlework, decorative articles, fancy- goods, and a varied assortment of useful I articles. There were, in addition, refreshment, fhwer,and market istalls,a fish pond,shooting gallery ' and autograph bedspread. To-day a rummage stall will be added. The stalls and stallholders were as follow : CONGREGATIONAL STALL. —Mesdames W Bennett, Richardson, John Houghton, White, Gandy, Lou- don, A Bennett, Miss Smitn and others. SUNDAY SCHOIL STALL.—•MeSdAM.S John Bennett, Wright, War 1, Mason, Thornton, and bliss Bennett, (Par Tree) ; Miss Mason, and others. REFRESHMENT STALL.—Mesclames James Bennett, Adamson, Elur chin, Andrews, Misses Ltiodon, Gandy, Emily Bennett, Bennett (Lyndhurst). Richardson, Andrews, Dtinkwater and deers. FLOWER STALL.—NIies Florence Bennett and Miss E Mason. Maltese STALL —Mesdames Dean, John Smith, Ez ard and W Smith. Rumsreoe RTALL.—(Stturday Only).—Mesdames J oh a Houghton, W Newton, and Critchley. TOFFEE BASKETS --NUMMI Mary and Lilian Wright. FISH POND,--Ntisaps Dale and Marjorie ESMIOCC. SHOOTING GALLERY—Mr Bert Nicholson. AUTOGRAPH BEDSPSEAD,-01rs Adaroaon and Miss Muriel Adamson. Some capital entertainments were provided in the annexe, including waxwork performances, under the management of Professor Jarley, assisted by his talented assistant" James." There was also a pig-drawing com- petition and a variety entertainment easel day at inter- vals, the artistes being Missee Mabel anel Jessie Clare, Miss Gertrude Jones, Mrs Hennan, Mr Baker, Mr Gough and others. Mr D.dakwetier also gave selections on the grameptime. A small, but efficient orchestra, with Mrs W B Roberts as conouctress, played selections each day. The follow- ing were the instrumentalists :-Ist Violins—bliss Edith Birchall (Leader), Miss BOachier, Miss Lees,bliss Wilson; 2id Violins—Mrs Willett, Miss Ethel Mason. Miss Elsie Taylor, Miss Johnson ; Birtles ; Piano —Miss Ethel Birtles. The following committee was responsible for the entertainments I—Dr Bennett, Messrs J E Richardsen, Leonard Bennett. Percy El Bennett, Frank White,Edw ard Gandy, John Jackson, B Riggall, B Nicholson. Toe onerous dutiss of secretaries to the bazaar were dis- charged by Mr J Gandy and Mr F Wright.Mr W Bennett was the treasurer, and the Rev U U &limns and Mr John Jackeon were responsihle for ths biz .ar hook. The Opening Ceremony. There was an encouraging attendance at the opening ceremony on Thursday lest,weq{, when Mrs J C Parr formally declared the bazaar open. Amongst those pre- Seat were the Rev Theodore Sista%) Rev H G Roberts, M A, Councillor A Bennett, M.LSCI W Bennett, E Richardson, Dr Bennett, J E Richardson, F Gandy, John Jackson, B Riggall, B Nicholson, F White and others. After the Magill; of a hymn and prayer by the Rev Theodore Bishop, The Rev a G Roberts said he was sure he was ex- pressing the sentiments of the stewards, offialale and the whole congregation connected with that church, in saying that it was with very great plea Sure 'tad cordiality they welcomed Mrs Parr amongst them. (Hear, hear.) They considered Mrs Parr's gracious acceptance of their invitation a very graceful and Christian act—an act which for more reasons than one helped to unite them in devotioo to their one common Lord and Master. (Elear, bear.) He was very pleased to say that Mrs Parr needed no words of introduction from him and he would now per- form the pleasing duty of asking her to declare the bazaar open. (Applause.), Mrs J C Pena said the part they had asked her to play was very small when compared with the work which had fallen upon many in connection with that bazaar. A great many kind triends had done their very best to provide the many things she saw before her and she hoped and trusted that still kinder friends might come forward and carry off all the articles and leave a handsome sum of money benind them. (Hear, heariand applause.) With every good wish for the success of the bszaar, she now declared it open. (Applause.) Miss Elsie Bennett:then steppel forward and presented Mrs Parr with a handsome bouquet, composed of lilies of the valley, white tulips and violets. Mrs Parr, in accepting tne gift, thanked the donors and said she had never had a bouquet given to her before. Mr William Bennett said he had the honour to propose a vote uf thanks to Mrs Parr hr so kindly coming a nougat them and opening the bazaar. She was not a member of their church, but she showed a broad-minded, sympathetic and philan- thropic disposition when She CtMe to help other de- nominations who were trying to do good. (Hear, hear). He was pleased ts say that the church-going people of that parish had always been very frieediy to the Wesleyans and when necessity had arisen they had helped each other. When the church people had a bazaar, the Wesleyans helped considerably in its success and the churchpirple returned the compliment wnen the Wesleysns had a bazaar. (Hear, hear.) For his own part, he could not see any reason why they should be C loggerl;eads. There was room and scope eneugh,for any church—by whatever denomination it might be called 116 —to do good. (Hear. hear.) Tocre was ample scope for everybody and it was a great act of courtesy and kindness' on her part in coming to open that bazaar. div.head: G.O. SMITH-ON INTERNATIONAL TEAMS.
div.p: G.O. SMITH-ON INTERNATIONAL TEAMS.

An illustrated interview with Mr G 0 Smith appears in the April number of the "Windsor Magazine," in which he gives his views on many matters interesting to footballers. "Mr Smith's first It match was against Ireland in 1893, when he was still a ' fresher' at Oxford. Interaational contests are popularly supposed to test a player's equanimity and coolness more than any other match, and 1 asked Mr Smith if this was his experience. Well, personally,' he replied, ' I think the tension is higher in the 'Varsity match, but opinions would differ about that. What affcts yoe in an International match, especially agenst Scotland. is the enormous crowd. When you come out on the field you see yourself surrounded by an illimitable sea of faces, and at first you can't help thinking tnat every one of the forty thousand odd spectators has come there for the special purpose of noting every blunder you make. But that feeling seen passes off, and I should think the average man is as cool in an International as he is in any other match. In the Varsity match the crowd is of course, smaller, but it is less impersonal, so to say. Among the spectators there are boats of people who are friends or acquaintances of the players, and many men find it mucti more difficult to play their best before their friends than among strangers. As we were on the sub- ject of International matches, I asked Mr Smith what he thought of the players who have represented Suotland in the last half-dozen International matches, as com- pared with those that have done duty for England. 'Speaking generally,' was his answer, • I should say that the Englishmen have been faster, but that the Scotsmen h4ve been more powerful. The teams that have played for Scotland for the lest four years have been made no of a very robast lot of men. Each man on the side looked a thorough athlete, sturdy and strong ; and as a rule, they have had any amount of grit and determina- tion, and were almost as teeth at the end of the game as at the beginning. English players, on the other hand, do not seem to run to the size or strength of their oppo- nents, especially in the forward line. To make up for this advantage we have bad to rely to a great extent on combination. Taking them all round, Englishmen pro- , bably have an advantage over the Scotsmen in pace, but this scarcely counterbalances the other qualities I have spoken of, and alone would be of small use. The great point about the English aides has nests their superior skill in c imbination, and it was undeubtedly this that gained them their victories in 1893 and 1890, the extra weight of the Scotch players being of no avail against the more accurate posiag of the Englishmen. Unsel- fishness in a player is always important, but it is doubly so in an International match, because the temptation to indulge in individual effort is so much greater than in an ordinary game. It is but human nature to wish to shine in the great mates of the year, and if a player can successfully bring off a magnificent piece of individual play, he is sure to make a great impression. lam aot suggesting for a moment tnat any Int( r iational player would prefer personal praise to the vic:ory of his side, but ha may sometimes imagine that a single-handed effort may be as StLICTSS3IiI as any other course, ant therefore follow it,ttiou4ti the other is far more likely to gain a point.'"

Wycliffe P.S.A. Society. A well-attended meeting of this society was held in Wycliffe Church on Sunday afternoon. Mr. David 0g en presided and spoke briefly on the text "Fear thou not for I am with thee" Isaiah 41, verse 10. The address was delivered by Mr. Fooks, of Liverpool. in which he referred to man's life as being typical of a ship starting on a voyage. He referred to the rocks and bidden dan- gers which were ahead, and warned his hearers against courting disaster by bad companionship, garnoling. drunkenness and social impurity.—The ladies of the choir sang a hymn, the man Hning in the chorus. Mr. Fayton, Mus Ban presided at the organ. Mr. B. Farrar, the boo sonretary, stared that the membership had now reached 427, and he bad hopes that this would be aug- mented to 500 before many Sundays passed.—The ser- vice was also taken part in by Mr. Healey and Mr J Willett.

Billiards.—Warrington Catholic Association v. Liverpool St. Marys Catholic Club. A very exciting billiard match, was played on Saturday evening, between teams representing the above clubs, at the Catholic Association rooms, Winwick-street. The games which were keenly contested throughout, ended in a most exciting finish, both teems having scored the same number Of points, 888, a most unusual occurrence in a billiard match. At. the close of the match both teams sat down to a substantial tea in the reading room. Mr o.roate spoke on behalf of the associa- tion and Mr Rooney replied for the visitor& The evening was afterwards spent in an enjoyable manner.
