div.head: MUSIC FOR .THE PEOPLE. I Annual Meeting of the Warrington
div.p: MUSIC FOR .THE PEOPLE. I Annual Meeting of the Warrington
Association of Bands.
Mr. T J DOWN presided at the annual meeting of the Warrington Association of Bands held on fuesday evening in the Town Hall.
REPORT AND BALANCE SHEET.

The lion. SItcRETARY (Mr B WaDswonra) sub- mitted the balance sheet which showed that the year was commenced with a balance in hand of £7 Os Id. The Corporation's contribution was .£6O. The expenditure amounted to £7l. of which £7O 15s was paid to the bands. Proceeding, the bon Secre- tary read his annual report as follows :—The bal- ance sheet shows that we commenced last year with a balance in hand of .£7 Os Id, while we com- mence this season with a debit balance of .£3 16s 64. , Thie means that we have spent .£ll more than our income, and have thus exhausted our reserve fund. I Of course this cannot continoe, and the only course I seems to me to try to get an increased grant, or give a smaller number of performances. Tula latter Course hardly seems advisable, seeing wnat plea. sure is giving to the people at a very small Cost. A. great number of people are attracted to our Park and open spaces by our performances, and it seems hard to deprive them of this pleasure when the average cost of ell the performances is less than 30s , a programme. Not one of the bands in our associa- tion would play in any other place for so small a sum, and no one now Considers that a band is actually paid for its services which receives 61 la man for a week evening performance. Men are quite willing to do the work freely, but often they have to lose time from their own work to appear in the Park. This is much more likely to be the case in a town of forges, See., than in a town which has a differ- outclass ad manufactures. A sum of not less than £7O per annum is required to give the same number of per- formances at the same rate of pay, or £9O per ennum if each man must have Is tor a week evening performance. During the year 49 performances have been given ; 22 on Sundays and 27 on week days. These have been given by the lellowine bands :—Volunteer, 7; Borough, 8: St Paul's, 8 ; League, 7; Buckley-street, 5; Crosfield'e, 6; Mr Down's, 3 ; Blue Coat School, 2; Monks Hall and Co.'s, 2; Padgate School, 1; total, 49! I would suggest that each bind provide one or two copies of programmes to ba placed on stands in good positions 80 as to give interested and intelligent listeners an I opportunity of knowing what is being played. I also make the usual request that any band playing on a Sun- , day let me have a copy of programme not later than 1 the previous Friday afternoon, and seed a copy to each of the newspapers in the town. I have to congratulate the bands for the punctuality shown in getting on the stand, and for the care they have taken to keep an appointment. As far oil can remember, no band failed to keep an appointment last season, nor did any band wish to be excused at the last moment. (Hear, hear.) The PRESIDENT, in moving the adoption of the report, , observed that from the statement just made by the I Secretary it was evident that the association had again dove good work during the past twelve months in the way of supplying music in the Park, and he trusted they might long be able to continue doing so, as it must give pleasure and add a little brightness to the lives of many who sorely needed it. In a large town like Warrington he was afraid there were many who had not the money to spare to pay for concert tickets who still appreciated good music. To such the performances in the Park must be a great boon, and must do something to afford them that necessary relaxation and recreation which were so essential to a healthy condition of body and mind. Last season 49 performances were given. These cost £7l, or on an average about £1 9s each. This did not seem to be an excessive coat, but it had unfortunately left them slightly in debt. A year ago they had a balance in hand of £7 Os Id. They had received from the Corporation • grout of £6O, and from the Bank 3s 5d for intere.t, making a total of £873; 6e. They hod spent, ea he had stated, £7l, or £3 16s 6d more than they possessed, and were indebted to the bank for that amount. They had now to consider what was to be done in the future. It was quite evident they would not be justified in running further into debt, and this, so far as he could see could only be avoided either by getting an increased grant from the Corporation, or by reducing the number of performances. It was a matter quite as much for the consideration of the Parks Committee as for the Bands Association, and he trusted they might be able to see their way to render them such assistance as would enable them to carry on the work as in former years; if they could not he was afraid they would be reluctantly compelled to give fewer perfor- mances!. He would suggest that the secretary be in- structed to lay the matter fully before the fown Hall and Parks committee in the hope that they might be able to grant them such. financial aid as would enable them to carry on successfully a work which was an un- mixed benefit to the community. He was sorry to notice that they had not so many bands in their list as they once had, and he sometimes feared that the love of Music in Warringtoa was sothewhat declining. He did not know how this was to be altered, but one thing struck him as being important, and that was, that those of them who did love good music and believed hilt as an innocent and elevating pursuit should not allow themselves to become disheartened or discouraged by what he trusted was only • temporary indifference on the part of a certain number of persons who at present appeared Co care more for cycling, football, soldiering, ' Ito., than for musio. They must hope for better times and a return to the musicsl enthusiasm of six or seven years ago. He Was sometimes inclined to think that Warrington of late years had had too much music, and that what c mkt be had so plentifully, and he might add ocs cheaply was not valued as it aught to be. The Wartiugten Musical Society had for years past been doing a most excellait work, but, judging from what he , read in the newspapers they did not meet with anything , like the sympathy and support they deserved and had a ,'right to expect. His own experiences had not always been of the most encouraging description. He never I appeared at concerts with his bands except in the cause I .of one or other of their charitable institutions, but ,neither the cause nor the music was apparently a sufficient attraction to fill the Parr Hall. The cheaper seats were usually crowded, but the higher. priced places were as usually nearly empty. He regretted very much that there should be this lack of sympathy on the part of those who ought to be the first and fore- most to support and encourage local musicians. This sort of thing had rather a tendency to take the enthusiasm out of a man, but as he had already said, their duty was not to let themselves become disheartened and it the Bands Association and other kindred institu- tions ‘ill stuck to their work be was hopeful that the day would yet come wnen music and musicians would be better appreciated in Warrington than they appeared to be just at present. (Hear, hear). The sssoulation was an excellent thing for keeping those who were left together, and hoped it would continue, and continue to prosper. (Applause). - -- --- -- ----
VOTES OF.THANIS TO THE OFFICERS.

Mr BRADY proposed and Mr AitarSTBolSo reconiod a cordial vote of thanks to the President,and it was unani- moualy agreed to. Mr DOWN, in acknowledging till complimentobserved that he bad often said and would repeat that there was no koiety in which tie felt so happy as in that of musicians, and none more so than in the society of membeis of the Warrington Bands Association. (Hear, hear.) He felt highly privileged to be tionnected with the association, to which be was very much indebted in many ways. A vote of thanks was passed to the Vice-Presidents,the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee, the Chief Con- stable, the Treasurer and Secretary and the Press. The PRESIDENT, in proposing the vote of thanks, said he did not know where the association would be were it not for Mr Wadawerth. There was nothing more certain than that he was the right man in the right place. (Hear, hear.) The association were very much indebted to him, and he should be specially mentioned in this vote of thanks, because he deserved all the gratitude they could give him. (Hear, hear.) Mr RICHARDSON seconded the vote of thanks. A DEPUTATION APPOINTED.

On the proposition of Mr itioey:-.IE-w—aa deeded to appoint a deputation consisting of Mr Wadsworth, Mr Armstrong and Er Smith to interview the Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee with the object of endeavour- ing to obtain an increased grant from the Corporation. 'The desirability of having the stand lighted and pro- vided with shutters was discussed. Mr DOWN stated that an estimate bad been prepared and it was found ithat the installation would cost £6O. It was considered that the expense was not worth the while. With reference to shutters, Mr Down promised to make further enquiries.

div.head: BORROWING A BOAT HORSE AT
div.p: BORROWING A BOAT HORSE AT
RUNCORN.
A Boy's Extraordinary Adventure.

At the Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, Frederick Shorrocks,aged 13, was charged with stealing a horse value £3O, and a bridle value 103, the property of Richard Barlow, at Runcorn, on the 26th March. From the evidence it appeared that the prisoner had been in the employ of Richard Barlow' captain of the boat Milicent, belonging to the Anderton Company. On Monday, the 25th March, Barlow arrived at Runcorn with a cargo of earthenware. The home was taken to the Anderton Co.'s stables in Percivars-lane,and it was seen there at nine o'clock the following morning. At noon it was missed, and the ostler was under the im- pression that it had been taken to the smithy. About 5.30 the same evening Barlow sent for the horse, and it was then discovered that it had got into the wrong hands. The matter was reported to the police, with the result that the horse was found at 9.30 p.m. in Mr Cunningham's stable yard,Orchard-lane, ' Pendleton, where it was being taken charge of. Shorrocks was found at his home at Patricroft about eight o'clock on Friday eight, but when charged said be had taken the horse for the purpose of travelling home and not with any felonious intent. In consequence of a boy telling him his grandmPther was ill, he took the horse for the purpose of travelling home to see her. It was subsequently found out that the boy's grandmother was not W.—The charge was ultimately withdrawn, and the boy dismissed with a caution as to hie conduct.

Important New Byelaws.
Tbe undermentioned byelawa have been made by ID School Attendance Committee for the County Borougb of Warrington :

div.head: CHILDREN TO ATTEND SCHOOL.
div.p: CHILDREN TO ATTEND SCHOOL.
The parent of every child of not less than fire, nor more than 14 years of age, shall cause such child to attend school, unless there be a reasonable excuse for non-attendance.
REASONABLE EXCUSES'

Any of the following reasons shall be a reasonable excuse. namely :—(a) Tbst the child ie under efficient instruction M sonic other manner. (b) That the child has been prevented from attending school by sickness or any unavoidable cause. (c) That there is no public elementary school open which the child Can attend within one and a half mites, measured seeording to ths nearest road from the residence of such child.
TIMES OF ATTRXDANCL

The time during which ev..ry child shall attend school shall be the whole time for which the schoool selected shall be open for the instruction of children of sirailar age, including the day fixed by His Majesty's Inspector for his annual visit.
PROVISO AS TO RELIGION AND LABOUR ACTS.

- Provided always that nothing in these bye laws—(a) Shall prevent the withdrawal oi any child from religiotui observance or I,:struct ion in religious subjects. (b) Shall require any child to attend school on any day exclusively set apart for religious observance by the religious body to which its parant belongs ; or (o) Shall have shy force or effect in so far as it may be contrary to anything contained in any Act for regulating the education at children employed in labour.
PHOVISO AS TO TOTAL EXIMPTION.

And provided always that— (a) A child between twelve and fourteen years of age shall not be required to attend school if such child has received a certileate from one of We M4jesty's Inspectors of Schools that it , has reached the seventh standard prescribed by the code I for the time being. (b) A child between twelve and fourteen years of age being beneficially employed to the satisfaction of tne Local Authority, shall not be required to artend school, if such child has received setertificate trom one of His Majesty's Inspectors of: Schools that it has reached the sixth standard prescribed by the code for the time being

div.head: PROVISO AS TO PARTIAL EISMPTION POR PIIRPOSEI3 OF
div.p: PROVISO AS TO PARTIAL EISMPTION POR PIIRPOSEI3 OF
EMPLOYMENT.

When a child between- twelve and fourteen years of age being beneficially employed to the satisfaction of the local authority, has either received a certificate from one of His Majesty's Inspectors of Schools that it has reached the fourth standard prescribed by the code for the tints bang, or obtained a certificate that it has made 300 attendances in not more than two schools in each year for five preceding years, whether consecutive or not Such child may,while regularly making five atteodances lin each week in which the school is open, be exempt from further attendance at school.
PENALTY.

Every parent who shall nut observe, or shall neglect or violate these bye laws, or any of them, shalt. upon conviction, be liable to a penalty not exceeding, witti the coats, twenty shillings for each offence.

Fon a Government Buyoreigner. ing of the which, when its members F were in Opposition, used to make periodical dashes against the iniquity of its predecessors in purchasing stores and goods from foreigners, the present combination of all the talents and all the virtues is remarkable. What has it not bought abroad during the war? It has had to purchase tinned foods for our soldiers, for- age for our horses, horses themselves, and all manner of miscellaneous stores and minor articles. Any Government would have had to do the same. It might have bought more horses at home, and encouraged some home industries a little more ex- tensively; but it could not have hoped to supply troops at the Cape without the assist- ance of foreign producers. But it has gone far beyond what was neoessary. It has given out bridge contracts to American firms, and justified its action on the ground of urgency. This was done in the Soudan, it has been done in Uganda, and it was about to be done in South Africa when public attention was called to the scandal. Had such things happened under a Liberal Govern-, ment, all the iron and steel-producing firms in the country would have been up in arms, and Tory patriots in the House of Commons would have been shrieking and behaving like Irish obstructives. A mild remonstrance has been all that has occurred however, under present conditions. We are of opinion, nevertheless, that the last experiment of the Government in this direction will prove to be the worst of all. We refer to the German guns. Some guns have been purchased that were being made for other Govern ments,and they have been of service in South Africa. We are not referring to them, as the plea of urgency might be raised, and it could not be resisted,though we must blame the Government for not having the guns in stock after the repeated warnings given by Sir Charles Dam: and others. The mean attempt to father on Sir H CAMPBELL-BA NNERILAN a re- duction of artillery made by his Tory predecessor has been already exposed. The guns to which we refer are guns used in troop. training, were bought in GIN many, bought in a hurry, and bought without sufficient inquiry. They are proving to be most unsatisfactory. They shoot well—and that is all we can say about them. They have every other defect guns can possibly have. They are always breaking down. The recoil action forces them into the earth where the ground is soft, and sends them spinning along for yards when theground is hard. Wheels are too low and too small, axle-trees too slight, and the mechanism needs abundant oil. The ammunition is dangerous, and it has to be discarded. At the present time the guns are as useless as old smooth- bores and muzzle-loaders. The experiment, in short, ha l been a failure. Gun manufacturers st

home could have turned out reliable and sound weapons by this time. But no, there was not time aid so these German weapons were purchased, to show how zealous and energetic the War Office could be. And the taxpayers have the i,leasure of knowing that their money has been thrown away.

The half-contempt with Agricultural Education, which a good deal of what is called agricultural educe tion is regarded by practical farmers is very natural, and there is no advantage in resenting it. It is founded upon a very reasonable basis. Very much of what is called agricultural education has so often been theoretical and almost valueless in ordinary farm work. It has not made a young man a better farmer, and it has not stored his mind with any considerable body of practicalknow- ledge. Probably, in some cases, it has made the college-trained farmer disposed to doubt the wis- dom of old methods without his being able to supplant them by something better and more scientific. He has got a paradox or two, and he rides them to death. Now, this is not what the advocates of better education have aimed at. Their first idea should not be to make the young man distrustful of old methods, and then to build upon this distrust a limited amount of what may be described as scientific faddism. His education should be practical, and it should concern every branch of farming. Pottering about with chemical analyses, never to be practised after leaving school or college, will not be of much ser- vice. He must be taught the management of stock, cropping, and the why and wherefore of plant and animal nutrition, so that when ke begins his real farm life he should be in advance of the young farmer who has been on the farm at home whilst he has been at school or college. Some regard should also be paid to the farming chem.c. teristic of the district in which he lives or is likely to live. It is here where County Council efforts are likely to be so valuable. Something should also be done to give the young men breadth of view by dealing with our various agri- cultural importations seriatim. Half-a-dozen lectures on the meat we import, and the sources of our foreign wheat supply, and the culti- vation of the dairy, and the poultry farms of other countries, would fire his mind to take up some form of competition. But some counties are doing very little in these directions. The wealthier southern counties are notoriously inert. They hardly seem to see the importance of any systematic elementary and practical form of agrio cultural education. Perhaps they may object to spending money to educate young fellows to go and live elsewhere. But all the counties that feed the great centres of population with young men of enterprise have been expending money of which others obtain the benefit, and unless all parts are. engaged in the same work there is no equalization of benefit. A. nationalieed system gives this equal- , ised benefit. Nothing else will do it so effectually Let us, therefore get rid of the notion that any-, ' body can farm well, or that farming is a gift and aot the result of education, or that science is something as remote from practice as it possibly can be, and then we may be doing good for our- , selves. One aim should;be to train men to in- crease and better all our bom3 food supplies, and to better themselves in the process.

Among the horrors that are to follow any exten. sive and permanent increase in the price of coal is a corresponding increase of mortality. The argu- ment of the medical paper which puts forward this prophecy is somewhat curious. When coals go up householders economise. There is a diminution of domestic warmth, "perhaps the most dangerous and most pernicious form which household economy can assume," and grievous sicknesses are, of course, the result. It is rather strange at this time of day to observe a medical paper holding forth on the advantages of artificial heat, instead of advising people to cultivate physical immunity against cold and all changes of weather. The outdoor treatment has a recognised place in therapeutics. Extended so as to make it the natural condition of life from the outset, the body becomes so familiar with climatic change that the latter carries with it no terrors, Thecultivation of this state of immunity is the advice we should have expected to see in scientific paper. Mankind is dependent for exis- tence upon too many extraneous things already without adding dependence on coals to the num- ber. Possibly the medical writer believes that wealth and ease and sloth have hopelessly en- slaved us, and that it is a waste of time to pro- scribe heroic remedies for people who will not or cannot take them.

The only disappointing feature in connection witk the annual meeting of the Warrington Asso- ciation of Bands wan the unfavourable balance sheet. Commencing the season with a balance in hand of £7, the last performance concluded with a deficit of £3 16s 6d, or in other words, the Association overspent its income by £lO. It will , be a source of regret if the Association which is doing so much to provide the working classes of 1 the town with that relaxation and recreation—so essential to a healthy condition of body and mind —is stultified by lack of funds. The only source of income is that derived from the Corporation, the grant last year amoutting to £6O. The num- ber of performances was 49 and the cost averaged about 29 shillings per programme. The Corpora. tion therefore gets music for the people at a very cheap rate. As Mr Wadsworth the secretary points out, not one of the bands in our associa- tion would play in any other place for so small a I sum, and no one now considers that a band id actually paid for its services which receives six- pence a man for a week evening performance." AO effort is very properly being made to induce the Corporation to increase the grant, but owing to the heavy calls on the rates this year it is questioo-. able whether the Town Hall, Park and BAtbd Committee will Eee their way clear to recommend a larger grant for bands. In that event, the onlY course open to the Bands Association will be W reduce the number of performances, a step which will be both unpopular and regrettable. -- Warrington Conservative Association held its annual meeting on Wednesday evening, last week and after the formal business of passing the reportd, and electing office' had bee, i carried out, a lot of selkongratulation was ,)clulged in. The Mamba, - and Mr John White also aired their views on locto and imperial politics, without imparting much in- lormation or advancing anything new. Both , made capital out the disturbance caused by thd Irish party in the House, and both prated of ths Liberal party'a disjointedness and want of leader ship. The speeches were really full of nothing but sickly platitudes and me6ningless, unconVino; ing phrases. With regard to the unity or want e_t it in party politics;` we should like to know bow,. Mr Pierpoint reconciles his criticisms with til: sorry spectacle of revolt and disunion in tht Government ranks which is presented at a1t005.; every Parliamentary division. The oppositi°"o presents a much more solid front than had th Government, since it Wii,t3 sent, back to powerSur, the understanding that "the war was over." ff-`„ John White thinks Liberalism is scotched in:WIIII rington, and Alderman Francomb attributes no% of the Conservative succe4s at the moral electl; to" the prominent part Sir Gilbert took." -- Easter holidays can never be relied upon for the ,oliditions necessary to a great out-door festival. It is the least re iable of the four appointed inter- vals for public cessation from the ordinary routine, th the exception of Christmas. Easter, however Is Welcome because it is the first break after the Zig spell of usually dreary weather beginning at rrtstmas. A genial Easter is, of course, a great roil to the millions of people whose good fortune " is to participate in its jovialities, and there is no l`eason at all why we should not now, haviog rss,d through a period of severe storm and stress, ok forward to a really serene and even warm spell 0f Weather, Even the most pessimistic of the ProPhets, after recent experiences, have been good '4ollgh to consid,r the outlook as not at all with- -4t hope, and when these meteorological seers un- 4e,nd, the mere " man in the street "is entitled to e courage Storm-beaten and weary, thousands 0▪ kpets ,ns throughout the country welcomed the 4,(lvent of April as the p ssible bringer of the kind Weather March had denied. There may be a few ✓oWflakes yet to come; they are not unknown to erhY D y; but one snowflake does not make a Winter any more than one swallow makes a sum- flier.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.

THE MALE VOICE CHOIR. At the Huyton Eisteddfod,on Saturday, the Run- corn Male Voice Choir were successful in carrying off the first prize(a silver medal)for the best render- ing of the" R,man Soldiers." Mr Robert Yates was the conductor. Five choirs competed.

PAINFUL ACCIDENT AT THE WIDNES FOUNDRY. A young man namsd Thomas Be Hard, aged 19, Ditton-road, Widnes, was following his employ- ment at the new stction of the Widnes Foundry Works on Friday evening, when about six o'clock his left hand got entangled in the machinery. Ills thumb, first finger, and a portion of the second finger were cru,hed off. Dr Donnelly attended to his injuries, and he was conveyed to the Accident Uuspi•Jal. MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN. The weekly conceit in connection with the above mission was given on Thursday evening in the in- stitute by Mr F Ellison's concen party. The atten- dance was only moderate. A good all-round pro- gramme Was given by the following:—Messrs F Kllison (humorist), Robinson, Eden, and Prince (violinist), and Mesdames Ellison and and Leach. At the close of the entertainment the artistes were cordially thanked, on the molion of Mr Snow seconded by Captain Reece.

div.head: PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.
div.p: PRESENTATION AT RUNCORN.

_ ' An interesting presentation took place at nazis- burst's Soap Works of the United Alkali Company on Saturday afternoon, The recipient was Mr R Baxter, a member of the office staff, who is leaving to take a more importent appointment at the works of Mr Thomas Cooper, Woolston, near Warrington. Mr Baxter who had served his apprenticeship at Llazlehurst's, was highly esteemed by the staff,who spontaneously decided to present him with a hand- some meerschaum pipe in cape and a silver match- box to testify in a small degree their appreciation of his character and ability. Mr William Heap, in making the presentation, ref irred in suitable terms to Mr Baxter's connection with Hazlehurst's Works and wished him every success in hi q new sphere of labour, a wish in which every member of the staff joined.

div.head: FIRE IT RUNCORN VICARAGE.
div.p: FIRE IT RUNCORN VICARAGE.

An alarming fire was dieclvered, on Saturday night, to have broken out in one of the bedrooms of Runcorn Vicarage, due, it is surmised, to the over- heating af the flues, whereby the wooden joists in the vicinity of the chimney ignited,and subsequent- ly broke out in flames, At first the Vicar(Rev Canon Wood) assisted by the domestics used their utmost exertions and battled heroically with the flames,but later the fire assumed such proportions as to neces- sitate the calling out of the local fire brigade. When they arrived the danger was soon overcome, but not before ..£6O worth of damage had been , caused. The damage is covered by insurance.

div.head: HOPE HALL,_ RUNCORN,
div.p: HOPE HALL,_ RUNCORN,

The weekly P.S.E. held last Saturday was pre- sided over by Mr Charles Beswick, who, during a short address,stated that he was very pleased to see such a gratifying attendance. He referred to the appeal for fresh regiments to go out to South Africa, and claimed that they were just as much Kioig's soldiers as those who went out there. They were needed to strengthen the ranks of those who were fighting against evil. The entertainment con- sisted orsongs by Miss M Greest, Mesdames Parkin- son, :and Bennett, and Messrs J Bazley, Broady, Greest, Woodier, aad Gatley ; recitations by lit.ssrs Faulkner, R Neish, J llughe4, H Greest, Mrs Findlow. and Misses E Greest, and FT Pugh. A. clariotiet solo was also given by Mr A Jonos. At the conclusion a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr Beswick fo, presiding, to which he responded in suitable terms.

REV' THOMAS WAUGH AT WIDNES. On Thur,day evening at the Victoria-road Chapel the Rev Thomas Waugh, Southport, connexional evangelist, delivered an interesting address on " Christianity and Amusement.," He said that the subject was one of the most important ones the Christian Church had to face. They needed amuse- ments, hut it was never safe for the ehild of God to touch amusements if he had to touch sin also: He believed in football kept in harmony with its original purpose, but it had become a great money-grabbing drink-encouraging, demoralizing institution Thousands read no other Bible than the football edition of a sporting newspaper. If they wanted to make the most of life they had nothing to spare for doubtful or dangerous amusements.—ln the absence of the Rev C E Stocks,M.A the Rev J Pedlar moved "That the meeting cordially welcome the report of Lord Peel, chairman of the Royal Cmamission, and expresses its hearty approval of its proposals and regrets that Mr Ritchie should have refused to consider the recommendations contained therein" —Mr Brown seconder-Land thought that before long there would be legislation on this important topic. —The re.solution was unanimously adopted, and it was decided to send copies to Colonel Hall Walker, MP. the Leader of the Howe of Commons, and Lord Peel.

Sr. PAUL'S WESLEY GUILD. A social and muNical evening was held in the Guild Parlour, Brunswick Schools, last Thursday evening, and as this was the last meeting of the session,there was a large gathering of members and friendQ. Mr E Taylor presided. The following at- tractive programme had been arranged by Miss Nor- man. Trio for flute . violin and piano, the Misses Harrison and Mr J Beck; song, "Out on the deep," Mr G-orge Pennington ; reading, Nis Clayden, LL..; song, "The children's home." Miss Taylor ; pianoforte duet, "The sleigh ride," Mrs Morrison and is IC Harrison; flute solo, Mr .1 Beck; song, "The outpost's vigil." Mr George Pennington; man- doline solo, Miss M Faulkner; reading, Miss Clay_ den, LL.A.; song, Miss Carter; trio for flute, violin and piano, the Misses Harrison and Mr J Beek. The Perna were much appreciated by the audience Durin an interval refreshments were banded round and at the close, a vote of thanks was prorosed by Mr George Hayes, and seconded by Mr,T Saunders to the ladies and gentleman who had taken part in the programme.

div.head: EXAMINER, THURSDAY, APRIL 4, 1901
div.p: THE EXAMINER, THURSDAY, APRIL 4, 1901
RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The above Council meets for the: usual monthly meeting, at 10 30 this morning at the Town Hall Runcorn, The business will inclade :—the passing of provisionally approved bye-laws for the control of the Runcorn iitiath and Runcorn Common, and the passing or the Market Accounts which show a total expenditure of £264 9s 164 and receipts to the amount of £265 91 71; leaving a balance of 193 91. The Finance Committee also recommend for adoption, "that application be made to the Public Works Loan Commissioners to lend the sum of £lO,OOO for 30 years, to enable the Council to meet the calls in respect of the shares to be sub- scribed under the Widnes and Runcorn Bridge Act," the directors of the Bridge Company having made application for £2,000 the first payment agreed upon. The date of the annual meeting will also be fixed.
BILLIARD M ATCH AT THE RUNCORN LIBERAL CLUB. . _..

There was a capital ittendance at the Liberal Club, Runcorn. on Toursday evening, to witness a unique and somewhat remarkable billiard match between Messrs Barlow of Frodsham, (a gentleman who had lately beaten Mr P. Quinn, of Widnes), and w B Brimelow (Runcorn), What made the game remarkable were the peculiar conditions. It was 500 up Mr Barlow conceding 150 to Mr Brimelow. The first half of the game being played with ivory balls and the second with " bonzoline " balls. When the fact is known that the ivory balls were very old balls, decidedly untrue,—the " spot " ball having two depressions in it. and a decided " spot," and the " white" with a piece out of its side—it is remark- able that such breaks as 25 and 29 were made by the Frodsham player, and that when he completed the first 250 he was within 40 of his opponent.' With the " composition," however, it was aeon seen that Mr. Brimelow had the advanta4e, and he increased his lead right through, and won rather easily. The final scores were: Mr Brimelow, 500; Mr Barlow, 437. Afterwards Mr. Barlow gave a very interesting series of finger shots" and dis- played a wonderful power over the b3lls.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES. [BY A CORRESPONDENT.]
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES. [BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

The new by elaws of the Runcorn School Board, which are now lying for inspection at the offices of the Board, should be profitably peruse 1 by the general public. It must never be forgotton that there is a class of people, in and around Runcom upon whom tne new regulations will press heavily so far at lea,t as the raising of the age limit to 14 years is concerned. Whilst a great deal can be said in favour of extending the time children should be compelled to partake of the joys of education, the conditions should always be made of eucla 4 natuto as to be compatible with the requirements of the poorer classes. The age limit raised to 14 years,plus the difficulties in the way of acquiring "exemp- tion," are going to make it hard for some of our poor people ; and methinks the Board would be better advised to have followed the example of the Rural District Council,and fixed the age limit at 13 years.

Why should I voice this contention? Firstly, because I can forsee the injusticea that are likely to arise and weigh heavily upon our poor neighbours, Secondly, education and educational facilities art beroming so get-at-able, that even before the age; or 13 years has been reae...hed, a " scholar has shown himself to be either likely or unlikely to benefit by a continuation of the process. He or shel has pronounced either " for" or " against " the I journey—wearisome and trying as it but too often is—up the steep hill of knowledge Consequently, as some of us must always provide the hewers of wood and the drawers of water, and I as it is more than probable we acquire sufficient education for such work at the age of 10 or 12 years, obviously, any longer time spent as grant- earning machines for Board or any other Smools is deal waste to the child, and a corresponding loss to the parent. Further the time might be put in usefully in commencing a textile or other industry apprenticeship, for which the child has a natural bent. Of course, to those who exhibit a desire to continue in school, their ability will have by the age of 13 fully earned for them scholarships enabling them to become acquainted with the inside of a higher grade school; and the 'better course would be for the School Board to make some suitable provision whereby assistance I could be given the parents of these children so that Ithey may continue in learning; rather than that they should glory over tl.e fact thot they will now be able (with the Justice's help) to fine them 20s if they refuse to earn "school pence."

Someone has the audacity to credit the Board "with taking prompt steps to meet the difficulty which arose in connection with the admission of, children of a certain age to Granville-street School.' Don't let the public mis-utidarstand me. What I want to do is to put the matter perfectly fairly. The Granville-street school is an infant school; and, so too, lam given to understand, are the Victoria- road school, at any rate it is alleird they were never formally converted from " infant " into " adult " schools. Mr. Thomas Saunders (a Nonconformist), finding himself obliged to send his child to a Church School, raise I objections, and demanded that the School Board should provide ' him with a place. This the Board could not do and MrSaunders was in due course threatened with legal proceedings. Mr W Handley (a member of the minority of the Board) then pointed out a way to solve the diffimlty, and at the same time use up some considerabie number of seats in the Granville- street School, which is beyond doubt too large for an infant school, by having it divided according to the Board of Education requirements and accommodation made for standard I. For the eccornplishment of this purpose plans have been prepared by Mr J Wildiog and submittad to the Board of Education; but the Board have not by any means displayed either promptitude or fore- sight in the matter,else a school attendance officers' census pins a little discretion would have provided for it when the Granville-street school was being repaired and altered.

The Runcorn Free Church Council which for 8) long after its d' creation," in the town wai practi- cally a nonentity, has at last taken its true stand in its true po,ition, and augurs well to become a force and influence for good. The change is doubt- less duo to the blessed mission only just concluded by the elution ; and as a result of which the churches have been drawn together in a bond of fellowship the unity of which is cemented in bonds of love. With the Rev A Wells for its presi- dent, I feel sure that the Free Church Council of Runcorn is about to become a living influence, end a cower ; anyhow, a contrast between the meeting last night, and a certain ono—which I will not mention—held about twelve months ago, shows ia an unmistakable degree that; a keener and more 1 intense longing for emancipation from pettv relig- ions differences animates the units who flock to. gather under the Council's banner of" Unity."

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

Snuffed out of the Cup Competition, excluded from the possibility of League honours. and trounced by Swinton in the Border Towns Cup Competition, Runcorn—once thought the finest Rugby combination in the ,world by some of us— very uninterestedly closes its season with the matches against Widnes and Rochdale Hornets res- pectively on April 6tn and 8-h (Saturday and Easter Monday. Let us hope that success may attend them on each occasion, and that " capittil " gates will accrue.—The Batley match is described lit extols° elsewhere.

Liberal Bazaar at Lymm. The bazaar in aid of the Lamm and District Liberal Association was opened again on Saturday in the C.mgregational Schoolroom. Not vrithsrand- ing the cold weather there was a good etendance, ihe accommodation of the room being severely tax; d, and there was ample evidence to lead one to believe that the la,t day's sale would be a success- ful one. The duty of opening the hazasr devolved upon Mr P W Killick, of Altrincham, of whom the Chairman (Mr G L Welford), spoke in warm terms. —Mr Killick, in opening the bazaar, sad be was very pla^Siid to learn what a great success it had been, and hoped the funds would again do well.— The P'allholders were exceedingly busy during the afr,rnoon and evening, and the concerts, phono- graph, and other amusements were well patronized. Ihe MUSig was supplied by Mr Kirkpa'rick's hand, who received hearty applause. The amount real- ized was nearly £lBO.

div.head: PRESENTATION AT "OLD BRUNSWICK" RUNCORN. The Recent Mission.
div.p: PRESENTATION AT "OLD BRUNSWICK" RUNCORN. The Recent Mission.

The meeting at " Old Brunswick " Schools, on Tues- day night, would provide anyone with an object lesson as illustrating the feeling of the Free Churches, of Run- corn, towards etch other. It 3 objct was twe-fetel,pro- vidiee as it did an opportunity for the Rev J B Foster (the Runcorn Free Church Council delegate) to the Nstional Council at Cardiff, to give an account of his stewardship ; and an opportunity for the Free Church Council of Runcorn Co tangibly recognise the work of the Rev A Wells, (naissioner) and the Rev J Osborne. , (secretary) for :heir services during the successful mission Just concluded. The attendance was a large one, and included : 'roe Revs A Wells, H Morrison, J B Foster, J Osborne, W A Eyre, and Messrs S Taylor, F J Norman, A R Norman, J M Frith, W Milliogton, R H Posnett, R Morris ike. The Rev .1 B verger took up the first pertim, of the meeting with his account of the National Confer. nce, and referred thaakfully to the spirit of friendliness and unanimity that prevailed amongst all the Free Churches. The Rev VA Eyre first expressed his thankfulness for the success of the Mission recently held in Runcorn. They had had a great draught of fishes,—(applawie)— but though it was so he was thaukful to say the net was not broken. (Applause.) Perhaps the greatest thing to be thankful for was the unity which prevailed between the Free Churches as the result of the mission—(hear' hiser,)— aid he trusted that feeling would be fostered. (Applitrie.) He sug- gested too that the Bible reading, as held during the mission should be continued, as their success and in- fluences for good hid been widespread. cHear. hear.) On behalf of the Executive of the Free Church Council, he had great pleasure in presenting the Rev J 0 +borne with s gold mounted Swann" Fountain pen—(bear. hear),—as some smell recognition of his services es their 'secretary. (Loud applause.) The Rev J Osborne then expressed the pleasure he felt at accepting the gift, which by the a- a e he took as one indication of his being rrguested to go on writing. (Laughter.) It was very kind of them, and he would highly appreciate the gift. (Applause.) Mr R H Posnett, (senior steward) then apoke of the mission and of the'magnificent way in which it had been carried out by the Rev A Wells. Subsequent to the bard work and strain of the mission their rev superintendent thou ht it would be well for himself and for his people if be took a week's complete holiday. During the week he was away from home they had a Free Chutch ' Council meeting and made him president. (Apolause). At that, meeting they also decided to make Mr Wells some sort of a present whereby he would be able to re- c the very blessed time they had had (3 pplause); 3nd it was put into his hands to see what Mr Wells would like. Acting on the principle, that to get to a man's mind you must get to the mind of his wife,tie then approached Mrs Wells and learnt eventually what would be accept- able. (Hear, heir.) Their present would then take the shape of a veil, handsome Gladstone bag and a travelling rug. (Loud applause.) He thought they would hardly present a bag and a rug unless a perm was going fivrayr tnit bey did Ert.waut that Construction put on their presents. (Loncl aeplause). They wished him every blessinganlevery health in the work he under. to urs_(sPlolause)—and hoped he would be blessed in his future work as its the mission just closed. (Loud applause). The Rev J Osborne, as secretary of the Free Church Council, then presented Mr Wells with a written record of 'gratitude and appreciation of hie services in the con- duct of the recent Runcorn Mission. (Applause.) Etbsuctou Could God an The Rev A Wells, who was very warmly received, said snaaids to speak as he would like to speak was a very difficult sternbthei ngi nem; Ind alwaysbe ext felter i 0 hr: could so 1 k md known tt n t o mendoi t ; it, a tender heart. (Applause.) Adversity or difficulties he could" buck up" againet—(laughter) —but whenever kindness was shown to him it always had the effect of unnerving him and he did not know bow to speak to them. He thanked them greatly. (Applause.) He regretted one thing, arid that was that the annual meeting of the Council had been held whilst he was away, because he had intended writing a letter to the Council, that should have been read at the meeting. He had consented to take the position of inissioner simply with the proviso that the Nonconformist ministers of the town gave him their earnest, hearty, and full support—(hear, hear)—and ha was there to say that if be had been the greatest missioner to be found in the ranks of any denomination, or if he had been the most prominent member of the Council of Churches, aed had come down especially to take the Mission at Runcorn, the ministers could not have given him a more earnest a intro hearty, a mere undivided, and a more sympa- thetic support than they had given him, (Applause.) He would look back on the mission as one of the brhrhtest he had ever held in his life. ('lear, hear.) He was thankful to God for the bringing together of the Church, and in a week or two they would have a special meeting of the Council, when be hoped to be able to lay before them a scheme, which he believed would be accepted, and Which would enable them to complete the work and reach those whom they had failed to bring in. (Loud applause.) He was very thankful to them for their pre- sents,for they had just given him what he most wanted, and whenever he used the articles he would think of and appreciate the spirit in which they were given. '(Loud applause). Refreshments were then partaken of. and adcfresses followed by the Rev H Morrison, and the Rev J Osborne on the unity of the churches. Musical items by a quartette party consisting of Misses Taylor and Birkett, and Messrs Knivetors and Birkett ; and by the Rev I Osborne and Mr R Morris were interspersed. Tee acornpanist was Miss Wells. The Dexology and B naediction closed the proceedings.
RUNCORN FREE CHURCH COUNCIL.

div.head: Mr. S. Taylor, J.P., on its Influence and Use.
div.p: Mr. S. Taylor, J.P., on its Influence and Use.
"The Age we live in," by the Rev. A. Wells.

The Old Brunswick School gave shelter to an apprecia- tive audience on Monday night, assembled for the pur- pose of hearing the Rev A Wells (president of the Free Church C mencil), deliver a lecture on "The Age we live in." The chair was taken by Mr S Taylor (an ex-Pre•i• dent of the Council), and he was supported,on the plat- form, by the Revs 13 Morrison, J B Foster. W Erre, J Osborne, and Messrs F J Norman, and R H Poan-tt. Mr S Toler, who to-1 the chair, said, really sp-otking it was for the president of the Free. Church Cline to take the chair at that meeting, and he was pleased to see the Rev Mr Wells present, for he svaa the pea.id of the Council, and could act in tne duel copacity of chairman and lecturer. (Hear, hear and anplause). deed, there was no one better qualified for the double capacity. (Hear, hear ) The proceeds of the lecture were to defray the exnenses of the Memorial servicas, which he felt sure, was an object to which every Non- conformist in Rune um would contribute his share. (Hear, hear.) Trose who had been at St Paul's ar d saw ' the mass of people assernbled there on that ocealion , would coacicde that the Nonconformists of Rtincern were true and loral—(applause)—and whPn the Noncon- fermists were asked to go to the Parish Church it fairly I seemed to him to he an insult to the whole Noncon formist body of Runcorn. (Hear hear, and applause) That some severe, intelligent. educated mini item were asked to go to the Parish Church. and Mt ' like dummies on a form really surpassed anything he could think of—it was an insult. (Applause). They might just as well have gone to Mr Morris' drapery shop, and borrowed seven dummies from him. (Loud laughter). Referring to the formation of the Free Church Council in Runcorn, Mr Taylor said since its eatablio. meant a grand work had been accomplished in the town. When the mission was decided upon it Was thought by some it would not be a SUCCO,R. bit Mr Wells and the other ministers Were fully determined to make it go and it did go. (Bear, hear). fl believed kr Wells ma not know what failure was, for whatever he undertook he carried through with so much determin •tion. (Applause). He warned them, however, that the work of the Free Church Council was not yet completed. Noneonformists and Nonconfermist children wanted protection. (Hear, hear). He was very glad to find one of their Nonconformist friends prepared to tike a stand with reference to the education of his child (Loud apelause).He was not a big man in stature—(laughter)— but be bad a lot of pluck and enterpriza. (Hear, hear.) BA warned them that if the Nenecieform- its of Runcorn did not mind they would lose possession of their own people. The School Beard of the town was now managed by a majority of people who were inter- ested in the denominational schoels and they should Be that such a condition of thinos was altered. (.Uear. hear.) The Free Church Council !should be determined to take the matter up, and if they did he was sure they would not let the grass grow under their feet. (Ap- plause.) He had great pleasure in introducing the lecturer to their notice. (Loud applause.) The Rev A Wells, having acknowledged the ovation aecosded him, delighted his hearers with many interest- tog things about the "Age we live in." He believed it was a golden age ; certainly, the most glorious age the world had ever known; and the cute regret he had was that it had not commenced SO years earlier. He alluded retrospectively to the advancement made in literature, arts, and scienv. Science was no longer feared as had been the case,and only seemrd more fully to establish the gospel and teachings of the Lord • Jerans Christ. Elucation was making gigantic strides • and he refuliated the ”oet's asoertion that s's a little knowledge is a dangerous thing," Rather should it be • said 40 a little learning was a good thing," and though . all could not drink deeply at first, it would load to the , time when the student could drink deeper and more . greedily of the good things of knowledge. The advance of invention and discovery was, tie nelieved, bet com- mencing • steam on land and sea was the eliminat or of distance and the servant of man ; and the lightning's (in the form of electricity) had also been brought down and controlled by the hand of man. The age they lived in was, however, more remarkable as the age . wherein genius, intellect and the power of the

e mind, were better recognised that they had ever been in the past. The great universities, the highest positions in the land (short of the throne) were all open and could be acquired by genius and perseverance. (Applause). They stood, as it were, on the border- land of an age of lights, and as yet had but partaken of the light of the morning. The lecturer 'spoke of the influence England had upon the age, its influence tor good, and its influence for evil. The Bible tad been translated into some 319 different language's and Carried into all parts of the world ; all being the production of the English Press. (Applause). He spolto of the tend- ency of the age towards pleasure,and warned his hearers to take care it did not eventually lead to sensuality and indolence. He spoke of the intense pressure at which , human beings laboured,saying it was not the amount of work but the pace at which they were obliged to work that killed. Was it not time for them to pull up a little. (Hear, hear.) He was glad to see tog that in this age war wai unpopular. (Applause). The 'question for them all as Christian workers was" What would their Lord and Master have them to do ? " and the conscient- ious fulfilling of the answer to the cpestion should be the keynote of their lives. At tha conclusi in of the lecture, which lasted considerably over an flour, the lecturer was accorded a hearty vote of appreciation. Mr Taylor. for presiding, wag thanked on the motion of the lecturer, seconded by the Rev J Osborne. The doxology and benediction clown the proceedings.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD MEETING.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD MEETING.

The ordinary monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Boardroom in the Town Hall on Taursday night. The Rev Canon Wood presided, and there were also pre- sent—Messrs E Inuson, J Pritchard, F J Norman, C J Cunningham, J Littler, the Rev Father Chambers, with Messrs J W Lightburn(clerk),and A Lightburn (assistant clerk).

div.head: SCTLOOL MANAGEMENT.
div.p: SCTLOOL MANAGEMENT.

Thc mutes of the Smoot Management Committee disclosed the interesting fact that plans for the altera- tion of Granville-street School as drawn up by Mr James Wilding (survesor), were to be submitted to the Board of Education for approval. This, no doubt, is a satisfactory move in the direction of solving the " accommodation (location."

THE HAIDAY QIIESTIONT. The Clerk pointed out it was his intention of getting the Board t) fix the midsummer holidays at an early date. It would be remembered last year, he hai written to several schools and societies asking them not to fix upon trips and excursions betv;een crtain dates, but to arrange for them within the peri)d of the holidays, so that children would not be wevented from attending school. Most of them had replied that the letter from the Board came too late,as arrangements had been made previously. t,By fixing the holidays at an early dxte, be Coped this year to secure the co•operation of all parties. Me Chairman observed the next meeting would be in time, and meanwhile the subject could be considered hv the School ManagemPnt Committee.--The tunal amount was passed for payment of salaries.

THE NEW BYE LAWS.--AGE LIMIT FOURTEEN. The Clerk explained, for the benefit of the public, that inatnediately after the seal of the Board had been fixed to the new bye-laws, an advertisement sroold bo inserted in one or more of the local papers for a month, advising the public that the same would be open for inspection at the Schaol Board offices. The public could inspect the original document and have copies gratis on application, and conic) lay any ot.jections to the same. If there were, however, no objections, he (the clerk) would make a statutory declaration as to their being duly advertised and no objection saisai to the which would be forwarded to the Bard of E lactation, and in due course the bye-la viz would he signed by the King and become law. The Chairman, commenting upon the new bye-laws said the main point was that the school age was raised from 13 to 14 years, and as benefiting the education of the people it would be a great advantage. Under the head of " reasonable excuses," the new bye-laws indi- cated it was not enough that a child should be Under some sort of instruction, but ttie word " efficient " was used. " That a child is under efficient instruction in some other manner" constituted a reasonable excuse, but it was for the Board and the Justices of the Peace to satisfy themselves that the instruction was of an " efficient " character. as there were cases, undoubtedly, where people had avoided the laws of the Board by sending their children to ,an ineffl:ient sahoel. An other point was " the tune of attendance ;" which was for " the whole time during which the school selected should be open " In other words a parent was at liberty to choose which school to send his or her child, but was not at liberty to send that child only a certain number of times. There was a tendency amongst certain people to believe that a sufficient number of attendances of a child was eight times a week. Yet there was no ground for such a be- lt- f• 411 e did not know who was to blame but he did think it was a pity there should he hundreds it: the dis- trict who only considered it essential that their children should attend eight times. The bye-law, now, however, made it clear it was the duty of every child to alead school,whenever the school was open, OF coarse, under the head of the next bye-law, it might be just as well to make an explanation. Practically speak- ing there was nothing in the byelaw@ whinh prevented the " withdrawal of any child from any religious observance or instruction In re- ligious subjects." Suppcse a child was °bagel to at tend a school where there was religious instruction or observance to which the parents took exception. The child would be obliged to be there, but the child would not be made to suffer and the parent would not in any way be slighted. This applied equally to Board and Voluntary Schools. Again, the Board would net require any child to attend school on any day exclusively set apart for religious observance by the religious body to which its parent belonged. Referring to the clause for exemption and partial exemption, which read thus : (a) "A child between 12 and 14 years of age shall not be re- quired to attend school if such child has received a cer- tificate from one of His Majesty's Inspectors of schools that it has reached the seventh standard prescribed be the Code for the time being." " '(h) A ehild between 13 and 14 years of age shewn to the satisfaction of the Local Authority to be beneficially employed shall not be required tn attend school if retch child has obtained a certificate that it has made 350 attendances after five years of age in not more than tw schools during each year for five years whether consecu- tive Or not"

Rev. Canon Wood pointed out that it was rather a 'difficult matter for a child to reach the 7de atandarel at the age of 12 years. To do so it would have t. be in the first standard at the age of sir years. With regard to the partial exemotion that too would be only obtainable if a child made 350 atVniances a vear for five yea's. This therefore. practically as•mred the attendance at school of children tint 114 years of age. It would be well also for parents to know that the magistrates would have power in the future to impose a file of no lees then 204 in the , case of persistent neglect. and perhaps it would not be quite so profitable for parents to pay the fine and retain he services of the child. and no doubt it was with this object in view that the amount of th, file was raised. The Rev Canon Wood then orow,sed th At the seal of the Board be fixed to the hyelawsortfch had already received the orovialonal approval of the Board of Edscatioa. Mr Cunningham seconded, and the motion was agreed to.

div.head: NOTES ON UAIVIES AND ATHLETICS:
div.p: NOTES ON UAIVIES AND ATHLETICS:
Rugby Football.

[By " Ovalist.l Once more the Warrington club figures io the semi- finals for the Northern Union Cup, and there are mare improbable things than that they will maintain their un- beaten record to the end. Few people outside Warring- ton expected that Bradford would be given their quietus on the Wilderspool grouad, though the Warring- ton club was known to be almost invinclble at home. But Bradford are the champions of Yorkshire, and have only twice sustained defeat in the whole course of the League corned:toe, so that it lo )k:1 very probable in- deed that they would prove too good for Warrington. There was plenty of justifi dole confidence locally in the Lancashire team, ho wever, for they have improved so mucn siace the cop competition commenced that their previous recprd is absolutoly nothing to go by. This the Bradfordians soon discovered and their defeat by 10 points to 8 points just about rem-den:a the game.

Warrington deserve the heartiest congratulatio.s for they were mucn the lightest team, had toe worst of the weather, and only their fair share of luck. Bradford looked a really awe-inspiring lot when they etepp d ou tie field. Their forwards were veritable giants, and it is questionable whether a finer specimen of humanity ever wore a football jersey than Hutt, the biggest mau in the visiting team. ro be only 21 years old, 6it. high, and weigh 15 stone 10 lba., is something to be proud of, especially as the weight was proportionately and evenly distributed. As several of the other men were not much less, it may be imagined that the home team looked a very juvenile crowd indeed. Weight is not everything, however, and the lithe representatives of Warrington proved themsielves superior in other directions if they were deficient in pushing power.

I • Tie match was every bit as exciting as the well- ' remembered struggle when Raid tx were given the order of the" oak" and I have m2t individu ds since who were so " worked-up '! in the second belt that they had no appetite for tea. Fortun ttely for me I am not afflicted that way and I have a clear recollection of doing justice to the good things provided. Peopla who cannot eat a good rir.al after seeing Warrington cover themselves with glory ought to forego the delights and exciremmts of cup-tie contests. Their partisanship probably makes it impossible for them to stay at home, so the tea must suffer.

There was a lot of hoping heel week, and most of it was in regard to the weather. The universal prayer at Warrington was for a fine dry day, and up to Friday at nom the to:Aid on looked lik ) being granted. Then it snowed. and k ipt up the dowof ill (sic) periistently. On Ssturday morning the sun shone, when the rein was not pouring down in torrents, and altogether the con— dition of things atmospherical was fir from holing eels- fac'.cry. So depressing was the weather that odds were laid on Bradford in many quarters where they were previously considered to have nn chance. The sanguine ones stuck to their guns, howrivei, and their confidence ?raved not to have been displaced.

I c Was a severe blow t ) the home crowd to learn. on reaching the ground, that almost at the last minute it had ben decided to leave Ronan) out, his ankle being unsife. So will has the full-bick been playing this season that one wondered how the team was going to escape defeat in his absentia. Tbir.re was no regular reserve man to call upon, and young Ratcliffe, the " A" team three-quarter, was deputed to fill a position he has only once before occupied. Llt me say at once that Ratcliffe's display was the surprise of the day. Ho fairly rose to the occasion and played in a style which gave confidence to the rest of the team and helped them materially in gaining so magnificent a victory. It might be.as well if Ratcliff a were given some practice in this department of the game, for his usefulness as a reserve man would then be much increased.

Warrington had the good fortune to win the toss, and Isherwood—whose captaincy throughout was worthy of high praise—did not hesitate to take the opportunity off,!red by a high wind and dry ground. It was clear that the home team would have to get all their scoring done early on, and they at once took up an attacking position. Bad judgment in kicking caused a lot of minors to be regiatered and valuable time wasted, but at last the homestsis found their feet. Fish, than& carefully watched, scored a brilliant try after one of the elickest bits of passing between Duckworth and Isherwood Inver saw,and then to the joy of the crowd Ritaffe kicked a lovely goal from touch. Five points of a lead was encouraging especially as the home bscks were making their presence felt whenever I the forwards obtained the ball. Broadley showed I donbtful judgment in coming out as extra half for he I bothered lldarsden and Wood without troubling War. rington very mach. Another try was soon forthcoming although several chances went a-begging in very alarm- ing fashion. Harris was the scorer. Duckworth making the oploing with one of his characteristic and unex- pected dribbles. Before the change of ends a penalty goal was kicked by Fish, and Colper scored for Brad. ford the only time they got well into the Warrington half.

A lead of only seven points did not seem very great, and Bradford set to in a fashion which boded ill for the leaders. They found the defence resolute and though the ball was continually in the hands ot the attackers they could not get through at all. Cooper managed a penalty goal, and then the gale came on. Rain, bail, and wind combined to assist the Yorkshiremen, but Warrington stack at it like heroes though nearly blinded with the blast. Time after time it seemed certain that Bradford would score bat a deadly War- rington tackler popped up in the nick of time always. There were only five minutes 0 play and the visitors worivid desperately hard, P,llard souring at the corner by a frantic leap which took him clean over Bate's head and caused him to sustain some injury. Cooper took the kick which meant a draw or defeat for his side, but there was no breathless excitement. It was excitement of quite another kind, and as a writer in the " Athletic News" says the lr.me partisans bahaved like a lot of bowling dervishes as Cooper kicked. Needless to say, he failed, and Warrington had won. Cheers rent the sir, made the welkin ring, and all ne rebt of it, for the locals were unfeignedly delighted.

Another writer in the "Manchester Guarditn,"thinks Bradford would have won on a dry, calm day. This is exactly contrary to my own opinion. If Warrington, the limhtlr team, coald get the bill and score more points than the stronger Bradforiians when the ground , was Ivavy, it stands to reason that they would he still I more eff ,ctive when the conditions favoured them. War- rington have shown frequently what they can do in fair ' weather, and on Saturday they would probably have blaten Bradford by tm points if the conditions had been the same as prevailed the previous week. Bradford were slewer behind, and bad no roan half so dangerous as F‘sh. Th +re was again some evidence of the super- iority of Lancashire football over Yorkshire football. What. may I ask, would have b'en the resu t had the Warrington backs played behind the Bradford forwards?

The home eight deserve all the praise they got for so pluckily tackling the visiting for- wards—quite the heavieat lot they bad met. The only way of get Ling the hall was by quick heeling-out. If there was .a push then Bradford WGII easily. Fell and Edmondson were the two best forwards on the field as far as individual excellence was concerned Boardman comes n'xt. He should certainly have scored instead of passing on one occasion. Forwards should always remember that they are forwards and are meant to go forward—straight for the lino. Duckworth this time was better than Bate, who frequently held the hall too long. The three-quarters wen all tip-top, and coming once/more to Rate ff I nine call attention to the brilliant save he made in the second half by taking the hall sideways, just as the flying Cooper came uptand kicking clear. He was well and deservedly cheered.

The Bradford back; were poor in combination. Wood vas very slow and hampered his young and brilliant cplleague, Mars ten, very much. The latter did excellent work, and the same may be said of Pollard and Eagers. Cooper was too much Lire a cat on hot bricks for my liking, and had he possessed the pluck might have pulled the game out of the fire himself. Ward was reliable, and the forwards did well without appearing P 0 exert themselves over-much. By the way 1 might just mention that Tom Bro‘dley was cautioned for a Piece of dirty play against trelreracm, which was much to his discredit as an 014 international and the skipper of the Bradford team. fie deliberately forced the young Warrington cmtre's face into the turf after be had been tackled.

Thoth tho orns,ther w g go tiorolithip there was a fin- crowd at Wildersplol and thr ororseds broke the rreerd. the sum received thr 'ugh the turnstilrs bring £223. This rvreantqcf a gate. o 8 000, Anl thpre wag clornra.,(l%tion for amthez 2000,, thanks to the " b%nking " put no during the week.

Unmixed eatisfAction will be ft-lt inWarrington that the 4eii-final in which the local club is concerned has been ailonAted to Broughton. A ground more convenient for the West Lancashire folic coold not have been chosen end they wilL no d mbt, ,tAgrnah!e, in large numbers on the 13th. Warrington wave in some trepidation test they would have to go to Fluddersheld again. but that f Ate he befAlko Oldham. and we grist] he rather inter- . sted jn the fate of the Lancashire champions against Hitler at Fartown: Soma peopte will naturally wonder how it ia that Warrington have won such favour ae to secure the seml-final in Lancashire in preference to Old- ham. Probably the reason is to be fousd in the desire (If the Yorkshiremen t ive Battey as good a chance as pessible, "fh Gallant Youths" are the only hope of the Tsker, now that the hi g and blooming Bradfordians have bumped.
Caatieford on Wednesday managed to get the better of the rviayed tie with Hull Kingston Rovers, scoring seven poi.,ts to two,

Warrington ought to wallop Castleford easily enough before a Lancisoire crowd and on such a good gromd as that of too Rangers. Arai then tor the final and the cup! The club will never have a better chance as hug as football remains to be played, for the run of ho.ne matches has been a phenomenal stroke of luck. Even should Old lam enter the final with Warriogton they are not sure to win the cup. In case the two Lancashire representatives are the sole survivors thm the final is to be played at Rochdale, but if either or both Batley and Castleford triumph, then Leeds will he the vacue. of the final tie.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
DEFRAUDING THE LONDON AND NORTIOVESTERN RAIL- WAY COMPANY.-THREE CASES AT WARRINgTON EXPENSIVE JOURNEYS.

At the Warrington Police Court on Friday, before e,e Mayor and other magistrates, three prosecutions were brought forward by the London and Nortb-Western Railway Company.—ln the first case, a young man named Joseph Jones, 2, Cook-street, Dragon Fields. Whiston, wag charged with travelling from Newton-le- Ili Blows to Warrington without previously paying the fare with intent to avoid payment, and also with giving a false name and address to an official of the railway nectinany.—Mr Fenna appeared on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and stated that defendant was at Rainhill on the afternoon of the 2nd just, and took a ticket for Earlestown. In addition to purchasing a ticket for himself he obtained a dog ticker. He arrived at Warrington at 820 p.m., and handed a dog ticket to the collector. The collector asked h:in where his own ticket was, and defendant replied I have not come by train.' I have been meeting the dog. It has been brougt by a friend, and he has gone on to Chester in the train. Detective Howells heard h:no make that statement, and did not believe it because Pti9r to the arrival of the train defendant was not en the platform. The guard on the train then came up and he stated that he saw defendant get into the train at Newton-le-Willows. Howells asked defendant for his name and address, and he gave it as Joe Roberts, 52, Battersby-lane, Warrington. It was subsequently ascer- tained that defendant resided at Whiston and was a stone mason working in the neighbourhood of Rainhib. —ln his evidence Detective Howells said defendant ban lodged at 50, Battersby-lane but left there abut eight weeks before.—A fine of 10s in each case with the alter.

native ot 14 days imprisonment was inflnted.—Harvey Phodes, a coal merchant and insurance agent,of Booth's Hill, Lymm, was charged with travelling from Arpley to Latchford on the 18th February witho4t paying the face.—Defendant said he had no intention to defraud.— !r Fenva, in opecing the case, said it seemed surprising tuat respectable men, for the lake of 11c1 would put themselves in this position. This was con- stantly lacing done by a number of people. I:l,3fendant .wss known .to _travel from Lymm

with reteirn tickets to Latchford. In some case's he would pay the excess fare between Arpley and Latch. fend. When he returned to Lyrren he ought to take another ticket between Arpley and Latchford. On the date in question he was seen to go through the booking- -ball to Arply Station to join the 5.17 train. He was care- fatty watched by a young man named Faircleugla who noticed that be did not go to the booring office. Fair- dough travelled on the train to Lymm and alightett immediately it stopped. He stepped Mtn a waiting-room an order to keep out of the defendant's view. &lbw.- quently he went on the platform and found the defend- aet had gone. Ho went into the coal yard and saw the defeadaot getting on to a coal waggon as if he were leoking after part of his business. L efendant did not pay the excess fare at the station and subsequently passed into the road. Fair- cough followed him and asked him if be had given up his ticket. Defeedant replied, "Yes, I have given it to Albert (a porter)." Fairclough said "I don't think you baee," and defendant felt in his pockets and said" Oi no, here is my ticket. I thought I had given it up.'' He then produced the return tag of a third class ticket from Latchford to Lymm iesued on January 16 h. The date In question was January 18 h. Fairclough asked him where be joined the train aad the defendant replied "at Latchford." Fairclough said, saw you get in at Arpley"and defendant said,"No I got in at Latchford to night?' Subsequently defendant told Detective [towels teat he thought Fairclough was a Lymm ticket cee- lector and that was why he made the false statemeet The Bench considered the case a very bad one and Imposed a penalty of 203 and costs (£2 03 6i).—Th. Mayor re- marked that it any cases of a similar nature, in which tee circumstances were the same, came nef ,re the Bench they should impose the full penalty-40i and costae—Amelia Bolt, 27. Richard Lathey, a youth residing at 28, Ellesmere- street,lappeared before the Warrington magistrates on Monday to answer to the ch irge ot furiously driving a horse and cart in Orford-lane on March 23rd.—Mr W II .1 Jenkins represented the defeudant.—Jotin Mather, a clerk living at 131, Orford-lane stated that at 1.15 on Saturday afternoon, March 23rd, he was proceeding along Orford-lane when he heard a vehicle coming behind him. Defendant was in charge of it and was driving at the rate of ten miles an hour. The vehicle was on the wrong side of the road for driving. A little girl named Elsie Robinson happened to be in the road and the horse and van ran over her. The defendant did not stop even then. Witness picked up the child and toiled she had a wound on the forehead which bled very mach. He obtained a cab and took her to the Infirmary where she was detained as an inpatient. For some time her life was despaired of.—Cross-examined by Mr Jenkins, witness said there was no othrr vehicle in the road at the time. —Corroborative evidence was given, one witness stating that defendant tried to pull up after the accident, but was unable to stop until the horse had gone another 40 yards.—For the deseoce,Mr Jenkics slid there seemed to be great conflict of evidence if the statements of his witnesses were true. His witnees would tell him that the youth was driving down Orford-line at a perfectly reason able pace. When near the end of Cobden-street there was another cart standing co the left side of the road, so that the defendant would have to drive round the back of the cart. He had to drive on the wrong aide of the road in order to pass that vehicle. Two other children were playing in the road and defendant had difficulty in getting out of their way. ,The girl Robinson ran across the foo.way and into the wheels of the cart. After the accident the def ,ndant went to the Infirmary to inquire what injury had been done, and to express his regret at the sad occurrence.—Defendant, Frederick Elitchen, Join Hoult and James Livesey gave evidence bearing out this statement.—The Bench conaidered the case proved and imposed a fine of 103.
