div.head: NORTHERN UNION CUP COMPETITION.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION CUP COMPETITION.

FOURTH ROUND. Warrington v. Bradford. The Yorkshire Champions Beaten. Probably the most important match in Saturday's ties for the Northern Union Cup was this one between Brad- ford and Warrington, on the ground of the latter club. Warrington had previously accounted for Leeds, Heck- mood wike, and L eels Perish Church, while Bradford's victims included Swinton, Holbeck, and Wakefield Trinity. Naturally tha visit of the Yorkshire champions to Warrington excited a huge amount of Interest, and though the weather was stoney and a lot of rain had fallen Jilting the morning, the crowd rolled up in large numbers,and there would be fully 10,000 present.'About 1,500 of those came with the visiting team. Toe War- rington ground dries well, and at 3.30 it was in capital condition for the game, while the weather had improved considerably. Mr. Oakland, of Wakefield, was the referee, and the teams were well represented. Warring- ton, however, had to deplore the absence of the full back, Hallam, owing to a sprained ankle, Ratcliffe, from the "A " team, taking his place. Toe teams were con- stituted as follows Bradford.—Ward, full back; Pollard, Eagere, Cooper and Heseltine, three-quarter backs; Wood and Marsden, hair-barks ; Broadley (captain), flutt, Liidlaw, Wright, Smalee, Feather, Robertson and Berraclough, forwards. Warrington.—Ratcliffe, full back ; Fish, Isherwood (captain), Deikenson, and Harris, three-quarter backs ; R Bate and Duckworth, half-backs ; Boardman, &len, Fell, Edmondson, Scholtze, Mereweather, Cunningham, and Swift, forwards. Warrington won the toss, and started with a Crowe wind behind them, Broadley setting the ball in motion. Fish returned, and the home forwards following up speedily settled play at the Bradford quarter. The Bradford men got the ball out, and Cooper carried play to the centre, only to see Harris register a minor with a long punt. Warrington had to kick very carefully to keep the bill in play, but by speedy work in the open they attacked. Edmondson ran and passed to Dickenson,who lost the ball in touch. Ward next came to grief, a moment's hesitation causing him to be upset 1 on the line. Matters were critical, and Broadley came ' out as an extra back. It was thrcu;h a strew; rush by him that the visitors' line was temporarily cleared. Warrineton would not be denied, and were soon back again, Fish making a fine dodgy run, which was only stopped near the line. Marsden made a mull, and the attack became very keen. Warrington got the ball from a scrimmage close in, and Deckworth threw to Isherwood, who /served Fish beautifully, the wing man sprinting in at the corner. Ratcliffe took the kick, and landed a goal from a difficult angle, amid great cheering. Bradford struggled hard,Marsden making great efforts to get his b Bele.' going, but the tackling on the other side was very keeu. Passing by the visitors' front rank at last took play to the centre, where Fish stayed progress with a mark. Coopir made a nice run down touch, and then Warrington Came back with a rush. Bate got hold near the line, and threw wide to Isherwood, who knocked on with a clear open- ing before him. Smart peering resulted in 11.11 ii being sent over the cerner flag. Rot work followed here, and Duckworth dribbled to the line for Harris to ground the ball. Ratcliffe missed the .goal. Ilia !- ford were kept on the defence, and for standing clearly off-side Eagere wail penalised, Fish increasine Warrington,s lead by kicking a goal. This rous -d Brad- ford, and a great dash took them to the home quarter. Marsden cleverly got away, and a timely pass to Coleer resulted in a try. Thoueh the position was easy Cover missed the goal, and half time arrived with Warrineton leading by ten plats te three. Swift restarted and the visitors soon forced their way to the horde line. Ratcliffe marked nicely, and then Rl- mandson led the way back to the Bradford half with a clinking run. Cooper had an abortive shot at goal front the centre. Fish gained further ground' and then the storm came, rain and hail falling in Oc- tants for a quarter of an hour. Warrington had it right in their teeth, but defended grimly. Bradford put all in, but with the exception of Marsien, the backs made poor use of the ball. The agile half tack looked a certain scorer once, hut DuiAworth brought him down a yard from the line. Play was very exciting, Bradford trine continuously on the attack and getting nessessien almest every time. Fell got off- side, and a penalty enabled Cooper to kick a goal. Great efforts were made on both sides, and Ratcliffe was cheered for a fine clearance. Bradford miseed many chances through faulty passing. Time wore on,and was only about five minutes to play when Bradford scrimmaged on the line. Maiden 'h-ew to Pollard,and the letter made a tremendous jump over Bete, and sewed, though he hurt himself. Excitement was intense as I Comer placed the ball for a goal kick at a moderate angle. He took great care, but the ball travelled just nutside, and the end came, Warringtoo, winning by ten points to sigh:. Final r—Warrington, two goals two tries (ten points) ; Bradford. ono goal two tries (eight point's).

div.head: Batley v. Runcorn.
div.p: Batley v. Runcorn.

The wretched weather which attended the playing of this important tie on the Mount-pleas int ground,Batley, ' had the effect of totally spoiling the gate, which, under Ilfav,urable circumstances. must easily hay broken all previous records. However, a sum of £2lB was not to 'be sneered at, and having regard to all the circurn- ' stances the respective treasurers of the contesting sides must have felt abundantly satisfied. The turf was in surprisingly fine condition when the teams faced each other as follows i Runclen Houghton. back ; D Jones, Butterworth, Richardson and H Jones, three-quarter hicks ; Jolley and Faulkner, half bacti ; Farmer, Walker, Reece, Lightfoot, J Langley, Tomlinson, S Langley, and Mes- senger. forwards.

- : Garner, back ; Davies, vitzgerald, Goodall, and Auty, three-quarter backs ; Oakland and Midgley, half backs ; Spurr, Fisher,dtubley,Flollingworth,Carroll, Maine, Rodgers,aad Judge, forwar is. Ref,reP. Mr aScCutoheon. Oldham ; touch-judges, Mr Knaggs, Leeds, and Mr Sedalia, Liversedge. "Runcora won the toss, and left Batley to play not only up the slope, but against the wind, and with a hrilliant sunlight in theie fa o; s. Litt r on, too, the 85.- (y youths had to face a blinding rain storm. Through i, all, hlwnvar the Tykes gave a splendid accouec of themselves, and had the satisfaction, for the tnird time in five seasons, of clearing the way to ths sem;-final. Locally, Runcorn had been lauded to the skies, and great things were fxpected at their hands. But, as events proved, Batley were also in excellent form, arid they declined to allow the Cestriana 10 have matters their own way. In the first portion of the game, the home back were speedily noticeable for clever play, Fitzorald Goodall, and Auty making a particularly good impres- sion. On the other side, however, Houghton and Jolley did great things in the kicking line, and the Batley dr- fenc t, always reckoned as amongst tho soundest in the county, was pretty well tested at times. With the ex- ception of Garner, every man did his duty nobly. First Davies and then Auty covered blunders by the full back and in that way Runcorn were successfully held at bay. until Jolley dropped a very neat goal. 1: was clearly evident in the succeeding play that the Batley for wards had the measure of their opponents, as upon wheeling the scrimmages n ,vr and again they seemed almost like running completely over the Run- corn backs. When the interval arrived Batley undoubt edly considered that they had done a good stroke of business in confining the visitors' score to a modest eouple of points. But on change of ends, there was a distinct change in the nucteorologicil conditions, the bret z beirg nothing near so strong as before. Some of the more enthusiastic partisans of the home fiftt en now looked to their favourites to attain a fairly easy victory, but they reckoned without taking into account the fine kicking abilities of Houghton and Jolley, Davies quickly essayed at goal from a mark and • penalty without any effect, the second kick being taken almost under the posts. These failures came as a painful surprise to oars: people, but, still, Batley were by no means discouraged, notwithstanding the fact that Runcorn rushed to the other end of the field, and Houghton and Jolley kicked as though their very lives almost dernded upon the result. But Runcorn's devices were all of no avail. Davies kicked beautifully several times fio.m touch, and as the result of one of therm pretty efforts a scrimmage ensued near the Oes trians' line. Here M.dgloy secured, and passed to Oakland, who ran trickily, and then handed to Goodall, This player seemed to have the line at his mercy, but he passed unselfishly to Davies, who stored a grand try and placed a remarkably fine goal from the touch-line side. This knocked the steam out of the visitors and Butterworth, Jolley, and Houghton kicked a wonderful length. Batley maintained a complete mastery of the situation, and woo with a little to spare by 5 points to 2. Probably the most pleasing feature of the display on the victorious side was the vastly improved form shown by Fitzgerald, Goodall, and Oakland. Davies was not so prominent as usual, but Auty was very useful. Garner was totally unreliable, while Midgley (Oakland's partner) played a creditable game. In the front rank, Fisher did a tremendous amount of work, though Rogers, Carroll, and Stubby were more showy. Spurr followed up quickly, but almost invariably failed to tackle his opponent. Jolley was probably the most successful individual exponent on the ground. His play in the second halt was entirely beyond psalm. 111 was

repeatedly cheered to the echo. Houghton is still a model full-back. The other members of the rear depart- ment did not realise anticipations, but this was not the result so much of lack of ability on their part, as to the merciless tackling and dogged persistence shown by the men opposite. Walker and Farmer were the pick of the scrimmagers. At the conclusion of the match wit m making his way to the conveyance for the head quarters, Jolley received a great ovation. He was hoisted shoulder high and carried to the conveyance amid great cheering and he was bailed as the best player who had evor appeared on Batley ground, Runcorn, however, played 50 per cent below their form. Jolly made the mistake of kicking from the scrimmage instead of opening out be game by those smart passing movements for which the team have become famous. It was a typical cup tie. Rick and rush were the order of the day and it was seldom &thee side did any passing worthy of the name. The quickest, smartest and the best bout of the afternoon gave Batley their try.

div.head: NOTES ON THE GAME.
div.p: NOTES ON THE GAME.
By" Old Ebor."

'The well known writer " Old Ebor "of the" York- shire Evening Post "thus cemmenrci on the game : It was difficult to realise that Mount Pleasant and all the surrounding kvjes last night were covered with snow to the depth of several inches. Rain and sun had ' done their work most effectively, and the white mantle had been completely washed and melted away. The football area presented almost a dry appearance, but this would probably turn out deceptive, for slipping football was almost inevitable under the circumstances, even on such a quick drying ground as Mount Pleasant. Important though the match was generally considered to be the crowd was not as large as expected, and had the visiting side been a Yorkshire club, the " gate " would have beec bigger. Runcorn is not a town that can send out heavy-laden trains of football enthusiasts, clever though the football of the Runcorn Club has been from the mid-,ighties to the present day. lam told that, beside' players and officials barely 20 persons have accompanied the Cheshire men to witness tho attack OFI the Batley stronghold. I gathered from conversation with one of the visitors' supporters, that they were fairly sanguine of victory to-day. The team have only lost two matches since the beginning of last December. These were both away at Broughton and Oldham respectively. On the Other hand, Batley had a good deal of self-reliance, for they rarely lose a match, especially a eup-tis at home. Young Auta , who had not played since the Huddersfield match, turned out again in the three-quarter line. It appears he has had a bona in the chest or ribs displaced, and a strapping of leather was required, it was said, to make him fit to-day. He took the place of Fozzsrd,who had his collar.bone broken at St Helens last weds. but for this injury Fozzard wodd have played to-day in the forwards. The selections of the Batley Old Band, played before the match began, were mach enjoyed. It is not often such a good programme, so admirably played, is prwided at • football field.

The wine, accompanied by rain showers, blew across the field with a bias in the direction of the "nine boil,' as the local footbell-eum-bavatelle players like to call the unpleasant (for the defending eidrhinw 'earner of the \lntuit Pleasant ground. Runcorn looked neat and smart in their dark green jerseys, and wore a nonfideee air when they stepped into the field etrrtly before 3 30 Batley played in white. When the two sides faced each other the attendanee, I should think, would he not more than 6 000 to 7,000 The doubling of meces of the stands left eumerous emp'y seats. Batley lost the toss, and Heughton consulted his colleaeues before deciding whether to play up or down the hill. The decision was to play downhill, and this meant that Batley had to start ie the face of a brilliant sun- The first few minutes' play was rather favourable to the visitnrs, whose backi indulged in short, sharp pass- ing on two eiccuioes, while Batley's first headway was made by a quirk forward rush and a sharp follow-up by Aiello. ft ee:genre, it was earls evident, was to be Bat- lay's paying eame, though the backs 4190 showed that they could run and pace well, for Oakland, Mickley, Fitzgerald, Goodall, and Ante' all handled the ball in quick and clever style. Weetie Davie., too, when called nn, made a brilliant save. Runcorn were penalised. The- Police Court and Prison Gate Mission, The foilowing is a summary of the principal por- tions of the work of the Police Court and Prison Gate Mission of the Liverpool Diocesan Branch of the Church of England Temperance Society for the month of March. During 269 visits to 26 police and petty sessional courts the members of the staff con- versed with 1,157 persons in the courts and bride- wells, of whom 768 were afterwards visited in their abodes, 76 women, 7 lads, were taken to homes, pro- vided with work, or restored to friends. Two other women were sent to the Society's Temperance ' Home. 37 tickets for worK at the Society's Fire- wood and Mat Factory were given to men and other work provided for nine. The magistrates die- ' charged into the care of the agents or obtained their help on behalf of 57 persons, and the police and court officials found them helpful in 62 cases ; 168 discharged prisoners visited the society's °Aces, and homes or the members of the staff tor work, advice, clothes, &c. In seven instances the loss of employment was averred by their efforts.' At the Walton Goal Mission Room, breakfa4t, advice, work were given to an aggrepate of 708 persons; 245 total abstinence pledges were administered in the work, 61 meetings addressed, 230 letters writ- ten on behalf of persons met at the police courts and prison gate, 71 visited in their abodes from the prisons. The names and addresses of 38 persons were sent to the clergy and ministers of religion for visitation. The cab stands, and shelters, lodging houses, canal boats, the races at Aintree and Hay- dock were also visited.

SEQUEL TO AN ACCIDEN WINWICK ASYLUM.

County Court Jury Disagree. For the first time since the opening ot the County Court in Palmyra Square the services of a jury were requiiitioned, in an action brought before the Court on Thursday. The case was one in which Peter Langton, farmer, of Winwick, sought to recover the sum of £3O us 61 damages for horses killed and injured, from Messrs Lockerbie and Wilkinson, Limited, engineers, Birmingham.—The defendants brought a counter-claim against the plaintiff for £l2, the cost of rep!acing two gates which they alleged were destroyed through the the negligence of the plaintiff's servants.—Mr H Rigby Swift, barrister (instructed by Mr H J Longton) appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendants ware repreeented by Mr Cave, barrister (instructed by Messrs Herd and Nutt, Birmingham).— His Honour Judge Bowen Rowlands, K. 0., was on the Bench.—The case for the plaintiff was that the defendants, Messrs Lockerbie and Wikinlson, Ltd, were contractors at the beginning of this year for some of the work which was rzoing on at Winwick Asylum. On the morning of the 25th of January, Mr Woodyatt, the representative for the firm, called upon Mr Longton and at his request, with the aid of two horses and some ;men, tgo waggons were drawn up into the Park. Nothing at all was said about the waggons being brought down again, except that as they were going up Mr Longton said semething to Woodyatt to the effect that bringing waggons down there would be a very dangerous thing. In the afternoon Mr Woodyat seemed to have gone to Mr Longton's house to see the plaintiff. Plaintiff was not there, and defendant went out for the purpose,"pre- sumably, of looking for him. As be was going he met two of Mr Longton's men, working two horses. He told them they were to go to the Park and bring the waggons which were taken up that morning. He said he had seen Mr Longton about it. One of the men asked if they must pull them up that evening and defendant answered" Yes pull them up this evening and be sharp about it." With these instructions. the men took the horses up and commenced to draw down the waggons from the Park, something went wrong with the brakes The waggons were loaded with scaff ,lcting and were a great weight.. The brakes did not work, and the waggons crashed down the incline. They ran into a gate at the railway line which someone had closed, and the horses were severely injured. One horse died a day or two afterwards and the other was laid up for some time. The horse which died was valued by Mr Longton at £25. The other horse was idle for nose days and Mr Longton asked for 83 a day compensation. There was damage done to the harness amounting to LI 104 and the veterinary surgeon's bill for attending the horses was 14s 61. The defence was that Longton contracted with Woodyatt to bring the waggons down, and was there- fore responsible for the damage sustained. After a protracted hearing, toe Jury retired but failed to agree upon a verdict, Counrel agreed le ace-pt the verdict of the maj)rity, with the result tbat ju Igment was entered for plaintiff with costs.

- - - was asked to stand as a candidate for the B lard of Guardians for Orford Ward, on the plea that more lady worivrs vine waned. for one was retiring, and ther would be but one lett. I was told that it was a moat useful, womanly and Christian work. I was will- ing to undertake it when assured that there was not likAy to be any oppnsition. Et3wever, there was. Still I was urged to persevere and not withdraw. I worked very h ‘rd myself and in canvassing the ward found the majority of the people in favour of another lady repre- senting them and promised me their support. They thoueht it was a lady's work to look after the poor and take an interest in the old women and sick ones. If all the voters had acted according to promise the rean/t would have been very different, but great influence was brought to bear on the election day.and so 801136 of the easily led ones passed over to the other side. It is the first election that I have had to do with, but, my word, there is great need for reform. I had my committee room and workers, but the sooner these out- side influences are done away with the better. If the people could pass in and out of the polling station and record their votes without being noticed by either side the !elm": would be, that more of the respectable, reading and thinking voters would turn up, The most striking feature on the election day was the number of men, from the poor to the rich, as well as a few councillors and ea-ceuncillors,who turned up in full force to fight against a lady.To me it seeoled incongruous unmanly. We are termed " the weaker sex," but I might have been a Goliath, the way they came up ; had I been a man they were trying to conquer it would not have seemed P o ungallant. But perhaps because I was a woman they fought all the harder. Some men are behind the times, and say it is a woman's place to stay at home, but the period is passed when women are to be bound down to the precincts of their own homes. A christian woman is not so selfish as to wish to devote all her time to those within her own domain, but is willing to stretch out a helping band to others. The field is open for woman and she now stands side by side with man in most positions The average woman is quick, intellectual, and clever, and will vindicate her rights if those rights are violated. I was asked to stand because I sdc workere were wanted .1 came:out on unpolitical grounds with a pure disinter- ested motive, willing to serve on the principles of christianity and ternper4nce. I thank my willing 'workers, also the 223 faithful ones who came to vote for um—Yours faithfully,
AGNE3 SIMPSON.
Lilac Villas, 104, Bewsey:;oad.

"Mercury "and the Trades Council. Sir,—When I ventured t put a few pertinent cries- tions relative to the local Trades and Labour Council and its action in regard to recent elntions, I little dreamt that I sbou'd be treated to such a shoal of grace- ful personal references as are contained in the spicy effusions of yeur correspondents of Saturday last. MY " ignorance," " want of intelligance " " ability to teach my grandmother to suck eggs." "weak head" "brilliant intellect " " gentlemanly instincts " " meaningless prattle "and my "ignorance at once comprehensive and astounding " furnish Mr Stott and Mr Flanagan, in lieu of argument, with the bulc of the material of which their windy epistles are composed. Their style of co,respoodence reminds one very much of a certain kind of liquid refreshment, which when de- prived of its "froth " leavas vary little of what is either useful or palatable for coniumption. I ventured in my last letter to suggest that which I new repeat, viz., that the intarforence of the Trades and Labour Council in the recent election of auditors, by the nomination of Mr Flanagan as a Trades Unionist, was a huge mis- take, because first of all no q iestion aff-ictirg Trades -Unionism as such was involvd,and also because no man who has the slightest acquaintance with the duriam of the office would for a moment allege that any candidate who is occunied practically exclusively in manual labour could possibly be as suitable a candidate as one whose business pursuit involves 3 comprehensive acquaintance

- with accounts. Apart from the question of fitness,there Is 'he Tiestion of consistency and this is the point where I think the tender skins of our coreespendesits have been pricked. Woilid either Mr Stott or Mr Flanagan tolerate the in- true ei of any other than " tradesman" into either of the " tradee "to which they respectively belong ? Is there a point upon which Trades Ueionisiei are stronger in their views or more emphatic in their enforcement thereat than the one to which I have referred? But Mr Flanagan sacs that the Trade Com el did not " run " him at the Auditors' election but simple gave him their " meral suppnrt" ; does that mean that Mr Flanagan was not supported " financially " by the Trades Council? If so I don't wonder at his annoyance and at the strength of some of his comments afterwards. The "moral support" of the Trades Council is evidently— judging by the results of the recent election of Guardians --e very doubtful q ready and those candidates seem to do best who get the least of it. How about the numbers of insurance agents who, as candidates at the recent guardians' election have de- tiered themselves as" supported" (I presume also only " morally " supported) by the Trades Council and con- sequently presumably members of this organization. Your correspondent " P.J." says there is " only oAe in- surance agent delegate i to that Council by his society." Well this may be correct, but it is also correct that one has noticed the names of a mueh larger number of in- surance agents who have been reported 89 speaking at various meetings of the Trades Couecil and my point is this-_I cannot coite see how a Trades and Labour Coun- cil which is supposed to be a representative body of "Trades Unionists" comes to include a clam of men who can hardly clatin, except as theorists to come into such a category. Certainly if insurance agents are qualified then travellers, shop assietants, clerks and a number of other men might claim to be admitted and the descrip- tive title of "Trades and Labour Council" would be en- tirely (as I think it is now partially) misleedieg. Even at the risk of again incurring the displeasure of your youthful correspondent Mr Stott, I would venture to suggest that the Teades and Labour Council would be much better employed in attending to sueh matters. as properly come within the scope of its legitimate enter prise rather than interfering on perfectly nnjustitleble grounds with questions in regard to which it has no direct connection. To Mr Flanagan I would sly that if be would write less, avoiding the tise of itigh sounding phraseology which he &es not thoroughly understand, and above all never attempt to interlard his effusions with incorrect French quotations, he may in course of time do 801710 public service with his pen. Yours Sze., MERCURY.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.
Alarming Railway Accident.

A Leeds telegram says that at Wellington Bridge, Helbeck, early on Wednesday morning on the N.E. Railway, a coal train was moving into the locomo- tive yard when it ran into a train of empty wag- gons. The coal trucks were thrown against the bridge,one side of wh'ch was knocked away and fell into the street. Three of the trucks were left hang- ing over the bridge. Breakdown gangs were soon on the scene to remove the obstruction. No personal injury was sustained,

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS:
Enemy Defeated by General
Dartnell.
Great Capture of Stock.
VRIMEID. TUESDAY;

On the 3lat ult. General Dartnell found a force of Boers under Eintett Grodelaar,al3 Henderson hold- ing a strong position at Solalleleel, 35 miles east- north-east of this place, and after some fighting forced them to retire east, after leaving five dead and several wounded on the field Ten prisoners were taken, and all the enemy's waggons and carts, and several thousand cattle and sheep were capured. The British loss was one man wounded.

div.head: Liverpool Volunteers leave Warrington for South Africa.
div.p: Liverpool Volunteers leave Warrington for South Africa.

The serviee draft of the s'h Irish Liverpool Volunteers who numbered 30, were allowed to leave Orford Bir - racks on Saturday in order that they might pay a last visit to their friend prior to their departure for the front. They returned on Sunday, and about noon on that day were inspected by Colonel Fitzherbert. It may 'be interesting to add that of the 30 volunteers, six of them had seen previous fighting in South Africa and had re-volunteered. The man, who wore khaki, and looked very fit and hardy. were paraded on the square at 215 on Monday morning. They marched out ot the barracks 3 little late..and traversed Marshhouse-laue,Or- ' ford lane,Pinner'a-brow,Tanners-lane,Froghall-fane,Cros- field-street, and then through Parker-street to Bank Quay Railway Station. They were under the command of Lioutenant Bailey: No time was wasted in entr lin- ing the men, the carriages in which they were to travel having been shultsd on the siding. Tney were very cheerful, and exchanged j ekes with each other. Colonel Byrne, the officer who commands the regiment in L•ver- pool, was present on the platform, and with the excep- tion of a few belated travellers the station was corn pleely deserted. The carriage was shunted on the 310 train to London, and when at 3 25 the train steamed out of the station, the men raised three hearty phoors for their colonel.

div.head: Warrington's Patriotic Sons.' Honouring the Third Contingent of
div.p: Warrington's Patriotic Sons.' Honouring the Third Contingent of
Volunteers.
Interest!ng Proceedings at the Town
Hall.

Warrington's appreciation of the loyalty and patriotism of the third contingent of Volunteers who have been accepted for active service in Smith Africa, found fotcible expression in the proceeding at the Town Hall on Saturday evening. At the in- vitation of the Mayor (Al lerman R3berta) the men were entertained t 3 a capital dinner, and passel a most enjoyable evening. The members of the C)na- I loftily, which was under the command of Captain Fairclough, wore their khaki uniforms, and from their smart and soldierly appearance it was evident that the three weeks' training in barracks had had a good eff-..ct upon them. A number of prominent townsmen were also present at the dinner includ- ing the Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Fairclough), tr Robert Pierpoint, M.P., the It ,ctor (Rev Canon 'Willis), Colonel Fitzherbert (commanding officer of the Bth and 40th Regimental Districts),Colonel C Ridgway (commanding officer of the let V B. South ' Laticaabire Regiment) Major and Adju'snt F M Floome, Captain Hutchinson, Sergeant Major Raw- linson, the Town Clerk (Mr J Lyon Whittle) and other members of the Corporation. _
-- Mr. Powys catered in his usual firsr-ela.ss style, and the various dishes were well served. After dinner the usual roast list wa. ennP through. The Mayor Proposes the Loyal Toasts.

The MAYOR said it was a very agreeable custom on occasions of that kind, when E iglishmen were gathered together on festive occasions—and be used the term Englishmen to signify Britisher in its widest and largest understanding. 0 toast the health of the reigning Sovereign. They had hardly yet recovered from tho feeling of sadness occasioned by the death of one of the nobleSt monarchs who ever sat upon the British thrones, but in these days when life moved along so quickly, they had hardly time to remember the scenes of yesterday bat had to betake themselves to the doings of to day. It was in that spirit that he naked them to driuk the health of King Elward the Seventh. We had every confidence in our King. Fortunately for us we were not like some of the countries in E Hope, where I the reigning dynasty was not so secure as it was in this land of ours. The King had Come to his heritage amidst the respectful congratulations of lie people from o is end of the Empire to the other and they fel certain that the splendid example he had had before his eyes during the whole of his life, in the unselfish devotion 0 duty and purity of life and c Induct which characterized his mother. and also in his father's splendid example as long as be lived among us, would nnt be without its effect upon his actioes and conduct. But they believed what he had already told them, that he was determined as tong as life should last to do all that lay in his power to promote the prosperity of his people and all that apper- tained to the good Government of his Empire. They i believed him and had confidence in him and he (the I Mayor) hoped and trusted that the King would be spared for many years to add to the continuance of the prosperity of the Empire. (Hear, bear.) The toast was enthusiastically honoured, a verse of " God save the Keg "being Rine with much fervour. In proposing " filer Majesty Queen Alexandra, their Royal EligtinessPs the Duke and Duchess of Cornwall and York. and the rest of the royal family " the Mayor said there never was a woman who so eempletely eapti• yated and held the affection of English people as Q leen Alexandra had done. Speaking of the royal family he said the country was neva so singu'arly and fortunately blessed than it was in the present reigning Einutn, and they hoped the reign would continue for many years to Come. The toast was heartily drunk

div.head: Bishops and Clergy and all Ministers of Religion.--The Rector and a " Justifiable War."
div.p: The Bishops and Clergy and all Ministers of Religion.--The Rector and a " Justifiable War."

Alderman FAIRCLOUGII propmed this toast. In responding, the RECTOR said they would have seen since the sad (loath of the late Lord 8i4P1,30 London what church work was, and he thought they would feel how strongly toose in authority recognizid the importance of appointing a practical working man to the post by the choice they had made of Bishop Win- nington Ingram, who was a workingman's bishop and had done a wonderful work. He should like to take ad- vantaee of the opportunity, as Rector and Chaplain to the Volunteers, of saying a word or two to the Volun- teers who were present that evening. Ho thoroughl7 appreciated their action. The men were leaving E -g- -land at the end of winter and were going to the Cape at the boc:aning of what was probably a much more , severe winter than ours, and they would not perhaps have the same comforta out there as they bad at home. I It had been said that the war was all at an end and there I was nothing for them to do. But they had been told tie ' war was coming to an end for a long time past. They I believed it W 4,. and he thought they all hoped it wao, even the Volunteers themselves for the higher reason, but there would doubtless be a great deal of work for them to do for a long time to come, fie wished to ex- press his appreciation of their action in desiring to go out to the front. He should like aloo to say that though he Watt a man of peace and not of war, yet he did believe this war to have been a very justifi ible and necessary war. When they read of the conduct of the Boers. their extreme nevo;rity and cruelty, could people think that their Government was a good one? Ein strongly believed that Ch. conduct of tho war on our side had been most humane. Re had read with the S retest interest and pains, the speeches made by Lori Roberts and others who had had opportunities of know- ing, and he thought they could all accepu their testi- monies to the humane conduct of those who had been fighting for uo. Re was sure the men who were now going out would try to emulate the conduct of the men who went out before them, and that they would not let their passions get the better of them it they

should lieii acon. He asked them to strive to act as men who were doing their duty and act as true soldiers of God at the same time as they were soldiers of thA King. (Applalse.) " The Navy, Army, and Reserve Forces.'

&source cf great annoyance and trouble and of some dan- ger, but one teing was (lute ce ' rtain and that was that the spirit of determinatioii which had characterized our nation for so many centuries, was by no means extinct. H thought that among the many good lessons wilich the war, terrible as it had been, had tanght them was the fact that there was still am lugs: them the same spirit of devotion to the demands of the country aid the Empire which charac- teriz el their forefathers. (Hear, bear, and applause.) In spite of the fact that we were a richer nation, and a nation in regard to whose life the luxuries of civilization had entered a little too largely, when the time of trial came the same spirit remained, the s itne uncotquerable spirit of E oglishmam, determined at all hazards to main- tain inviolable the splendid anti, magnificent traditiont which had been banded down to us from the past. (Hear, hear, and applause.) With regard to the kind references which had been made to himself be wished to say that it 'would have been utterly impossible for, him, however anxious be might have been to do all he could as an Wielded( to have accomplished !any- thing like *hat had been'. accomplished during the past 18 months if be bad , not been supported most nobly and most generously by practically the whole of his fellow-townsmen. The or innest rempent of hia life had ben when be had realised how trate loyal and henry had been the dev >doe of his fellow.townsmen. His Worship made complimentary 4inisions to Captain apoleton, Lieutenan Cary, and Captain Fairclough, and add lon b.lieved that all the men present under the leadership of C iptain Feirclough would see to it that the reputation of the town, of themael yes, arid of the battalion, was fully maintained as far as it lay in their power. (Applause.) The toast was eethualastic ally drunk. Captain Fateceotroa briefly responded. Since they had been at the barracks the company had done a great deal of work.end it seemee to him that they had covered a lot of ground-0 sughter)—but personally the training had done him no narrn. The speak ,r said he was per- sonally obiieed te Cceonel Fitzherbert for the kind words be had spoken as to the behaviour of the men ; it was a pleasure to work with such men, as there had been no treuele whatever. A better set of men he did not wish to have anything to do with. Ha colloid-led by saltine the c ettintreet to give three hearty cheers for the men and Corporation. the Town Clerk, and the Borough Treasurer for the kind tees which had been shown to the VAnnt,ers in chi, preparation of the life policies—especi- ally to the Town Clerk, for his assistance in legal matters.

M PIERPOINT oraposed the he,,, to of the Mayor, who he said had displayed an energy duriag his term of office which he did not think could have been sutpasised. He had placed himself at the head of every good move- ment far the benefit of the men who had gone to South Africa and the men who were about to go out, and he was deserving of all praise. He was sure the town appreciated his self-devotion, his industry, and his courage. (App'ause.) The toast was received with mosicol honours, cheers being given for the Mayoress an i family. div.head: Proposed Soldiers' Club for Warrington,
div.p: Proposed Soldiers' Club for Warrington,

Mr R PIERPOINT Xl P., prop - :s 'd tire next tnaat—that of the " Navy, army and reterve forces." Referring to the navy be said be need not dilate upon its ,greatneso land power. It pervaded the whole world and was com- posed of mighty ships filled with valiant men, valiant sailors and btave officers. . L ink at what the sailors had done in the war which was now drawing to a close. He (red not tell them what they had done, what they did under Captain Lambton for Ladysmith, and of their willing- ness when the opportunity Came for them to do the , hardest work they could for King andoountry Speak- ing of the army he said they had seen from in antis to month, almost from year to year, the self devo •n, self sacrifice,the bravery and the hard work which tee army had done in South Afriea, and in China and were reads* to do in any other part of the world. Let them not fdr- get that the army was being asked to go to war almost very month. We wire alwatti hav- ing our little ware or great was in tome country or other. It might be in lodia on the Northwest Frontier' it might be in South Africa as it was now, it might be on the west coast of Africa, or in China, but whenever our army was asked to go nut it responded to the asking in the true spirit of its fathers and grandfathers. But that evening thee were chiily concerned with the third item of the toast—the reserve forces. He thought 'hey might well congratulate them • selves upon what Warrington and its Volunteer Corps had done for the army at the front. (Applause.) He would not arrogate to themselves that they had done better than any other towo but te rho ight he was right in asserting that no other town had done better than this town. (Applause.) He did not profess to assign the reasons but ne thought there was a great reason in this —that Warrington was en old town, a somewhat old fashioned town, a very large and important and a com- pact town, and it had fortunately at the head of Re Municipal Council a May ir who had taken the greatest interest in, and had devoted himself with the greatest energy to the requirements of the Volunteers who volun- teered for service abroad. (Applause.) He ventured to say before his face that the Mayor had been of the greatest value to the town during this trying period— (hear, hear,)—and that he had set an example which had been followed by the whole town in furthering the interests of the volunteers who were going to the front. He congratulated the town that it was sending a third detachment to the front to join those brave fellows who had gone before them, and devoted themselves to the exigences of their country He felt excessively proud, having the high honour of re- presenting this town in Parliament, that Warrington had done and was doing so well and be hoped it would not be long before he should have the opportunity of congratulating Captain Appleton and these who were with him, on their return to their native land. ( epplause). In conclusion he expressed the hope that It would not be long before the Mayor and all of them would have the opportunity of shaking the men who were going out by the band and saying " Thank G)d you have come back to us safe and sound." (Hear. hear). .

_ , COLONEL FITZREREERT, in responding sstid that the conduct of the detachment, during the whole of the time they had been in the Birraeke had given the most complete sitisfaction. Nothing could have been better than the behaviour of the men ; they had Peen willing and anxious to learn. He thought they had given the men perhaps rather a hard time of it but he did not think they regretted that, and he was of opinion that they were 50 per cent better than when they marched through the Barracks Gate. (&pplauee ) Con- tinuing he referred to the kindness and thought- fulness which had iron shown to soldiers ordered to the front, by the people of Lanchaehire, and said that Warringtoo had perhaps stood as high as any other town in its generosity and kindness to it 4 soldiers. Among the many gallant deeds of eoldiers during the ' war, he did not thief; that one had brought more sorrow I or perhaps more pride to the people of Warrington than I the gallant death of Colonel O'Leary of the South Lanca- shire Regiment, who was a friend to many of them. As regarded the reserve forces he (the speaker) thought the war had brought very much together the reserve and eo'diers of the general line, and perhaps to the g sat advantage of both. Their General had ' now put forward a scheme which he thought wou'd commend itself to them, and one which could not be carried out without the co-operation of the Mayor and Corpor ttion and their fellow citizens. It was proposed to start in Warringten a soldiers' club. At present there wee no place to which a Man could go when he wee out of barracks, and the result was that he wandered about the town and sometimes went to heusee whichnt would have been letter for him to have left alone. They required a:place where volunteers and soldiers could meet together,—a respectable and well conducted club. It would not be a refuge or home but a club where they could all meet on one common level and talk together of any subjects of interest. The proposal of the General was that the club should be entirely undenominational—a club in its pure Sense— and it might please the Mayor to hear that it was pr- posed that no alcoholic liquors should be sold there. He ' hoped the club weuld be in full working crder by the time the men returned from the front and be had no doubt that thi Mayor and Member would be happy to greet some of them chere. (Applause.) In conclusion he asked the volunteers to bear themselves as gallant men and brave Englishmen in actien and expressed the hope that they might come back safe and sound to the old country. (App'ause.) Colonel RIDGWAY also responded and alluded to the death of the late Colonel O'Leary, who, he said was one of the battalion's Iva friends. He was a min whom they loved and a man who did as much for the battalion as any man in Warrington. He did hisbest as a soldier ant when the time came for him to go out and die for his country, he did so and died most nobly. No one reeretted Ws death more than the men of the F rse Volunteer Battalion South Lencashire Regiment. During ' I the past twelve months they had had a new experience. Lest Septemb‘r he (the colonel) called the battalion ' together to ark them to volunteer to form a company to ' go out to the front. 113 thought it was perhaps a hold experiment and he did not know bow the War Orli to would receive it, but he thought it was time that the V elunteers showed what they were made of. Well, on 1 that night,they did show what they were made of They I I came forward and he found he should have no ' I difficulty in raising a company. He broached the I question to the War Office authorities, Feasibly they were surprised at such a thing arid replied that it was not their intention to send out Volunteers ' But on the 9:h October, when e r Kruger said he would drive the British out of Scoth Africa they gave the b Malice] a chance and the men who went out before 1 the present detachment came forward. They went to I the front and from the report he had received from , Colonel Hall, he was very pleased sal proud to say they had carried out their duty in a manner which had boon I pleasing to him and an honcaar to the town net Warring- I ton. The battalion also sent out another section aad , they lead also done well. Some were still with their company, and some of theta perhaps finding the infantry a little monotonous. had joined the mounted infantry. One officer, Lieutenant Cary, was at Pretoria with some of his men the lase time he (the colonel) heard of him. He felt that the men who were now going to the front would do their duty, They were tit in every way for a soldier's life, and he was Sure that under the command of Captain Fairclough and with Ser geant Thorniley and the other non-cemmiesioned officer they would de their best. He tieped they might go out at an early date and when they got out that the war mielet soon be over and that they would come back once more to old Eegland. The Colonel proceeded to refer i'l felicitous terms to the assistance which had been rendered to thrs bittalien be the Merry and Mr R Pierpoint and in conclusion expressed his approval of the echecnt for the establishment of a club for soldiers and volunteers. He should be very glad to take part in assisting any move- ment of that character because he thought that the institution was nece,sery in a large garrison town. div.head: "Violet" Bazaar at Padgate.
div.p: The "Violet" Bazaar at Padgate.

The "Violet" bazaar was opened on Saturday in the Padgate Wesleyan Schoolroom.for the third and last day's sale by the Rey H G Roberts who was accompanied on the platform by the Rev T Bishop. Sir Bishop sail he was sure they would be pleased to welcome his friend the Rev H G Roberts. He nee led no introduction ; he was well known to them all.—Tha Rev H G Roberts expressed his thanks to his superintendent for the kind manner in which he had introduced him. That was a new rile for him the speaker to play. He hoped that the last day would be the beat. Their efforts had been crowned with success. He trusted that the stalls would be cleared of their contents before the close of the bsz lar, but if they were not, it was the inten- tion of the committee to hold a garden fete in the summer. Miss Lilian Wright presented the rev. gen'lemsn with a buttonhole, and before the sales proceeded Miss Emily Bennett (Westlands),general secretary of the P idgate branch .of the Wesleyan ' Guild, presented Mr Roberts with a framed picture on behalf of the msmbers of the guild, of which society he is the president.-7‘frs John Bennett, in proposinz a vote of thanks to Jr Roberts, said they had not only to thank him for having opened the bazaar that day, but also for the work he had done in connection witi the organization of it. They owed him a great debt of gratitude for the various institutions he had helped forward at their church during his ministry in the Warrington circuit.— Mrs Edwin Richardson seconded the vote of thanks which was carried with acclamation.—At the close of what has proved a most succeslful bazaar, it was announce 1 that the sum of .£371 63 10 had been realized.

div.head: THE. CENSUS. Newton and Earlestown.
div.p: THE. CENSUS. Newton and Earlestown.

In the Newton district the collection of the census ! papers was unattendei by any untoward incident. In the inajlrity of cases the people were willing to assist the enumerators as mach as possible, and the papers were filled up with a fair degree of accuracy. One of the entlmeraters on Sunday had a lively egperience. It was ' port of his duty to visit any barges which might be lying upon the canal in the Newton district, and fulfill- ing this duty in the-afternoon, he had visited one barge. and was returning to terrafirma in a small boat, and when ste poi crifrona the boat to the canal bank, he aced. dentally fell into the water, with the result that be got a'wettin,g, which proved inc.re striltine than pleasant. He has v ,wed not to have anychrig to do with the census again.

div.head: Rev. J. Yonge draws a Lesson
div.p: The Rev. J. Yonge draws a Lesson

from the Census. Tu, Rev John Yonge base4hia morning discourse at Wycliffe Congregational Chain on Sunday, on the text "The Lord shall count when He writeth up the peoples, this one was born there" (Psalm 87 verse 6). Every inhabitant of the United Kingdom, he said, would be made to remember and specify the place where he was born in connection with the census. It mattered not bow lordly, or how lowly, his birth might have been ; whether it took place in a mansion or in a cottage. lo was by no means the lot of every individual to have any special reason to exult concerning the place of his birth. Yet how often was it true that the plEbian had in reality a nobler and a truer ancestry Wan the titled noble! Fne humbler ancestry was often parer, immeasurably more tionourab e, and therefore more, as the saying was, to " proud of." E itthly station was not always indi- cative of personal worth. If" worth" could be strictly SD Ideated the lefty and the lowly would have to make many an exchange of positions. Apart, however, from pride or humility of birth in these respects, there had ever been in the history of the evorld,couotries,kingdoma empires, to have been born in which,had been regarded as peculiar advantage, satisfaction and pride. The member of the Hebrew race had ever been proud of Ins race and ancestry. The ancient Roman was accus- tomed to boast of his citizenship in the "first empire of the world." 'roe sons of all countries, indeed, had come to this feeling of natural love fee fatherland, and it was I inspiring the men of to-day in all lands with manifold eoterprise and courage. Every member of these three kingdoms—England, Scotland, Ireland, and the little principality of Wales—was proud of the land of his birth, and proud of citizenship in an empire upon which the sun never set. Nearly every man and woman—as they looked back that census Sunday to the place where first they saw the light— would, if they were at all reflective, be :sensible of e feeling of sympathetic and affectionate interest in that particular place. And if their birthplace had, for any reason, found enviable distinction, they would be proul of their connection with it. Lancashire folk were proud of their county, and Londoners like himself were pronl of their birth in the greatest city in the world. Bat in the tent and in the Psalm there was :suggested a 801 higher an t nobler" pride of birth "—birth in the ciry of, God. And there seemed also to be set forth a far no ore marvellous and interesting census or record than that which was being accomplished in these kingdoms. It seemed to speak of God counting up the peoples—taking ' His ultimate and final census of those who were citizens of His Kilogl,m, and He was recording about them that theirs was the citizenship of birth, or, at any rate of second birth. Toe question asked by the National census might lift their thoughts to the other and the higher and the diviner. " Where born ? " Was ouf birth only of this lower life; of this earthly sphere P Was our citizenship that alone of this kingdom arid em- pire ? Had we as yet no conscious heti upon" things unseen ?" Had we no title to the mansion in the skies ? Had we not made submission to toe King of kings ? Were we still unmentioned on the burgess roll, the mil. versal cosmopolitan roll of Heaven ? This was the ques- tion high over all other. And it suggested tne businee hat should be seen to and settled this census' day.

div.head: EARLESTOWN BURGLARIES -- Prisoner Committed for Trial.
div.p: THE EARLESTOWN BURGLARIES -- Prisoner Committed for Trial.
Interesting Details of the Affair.

At the VVarrington Occasional Court on Tuesday, be- fore Mr F A Frost, JAM:+I Anderson, alias Ward, was eh aged with breaking and entering the shop of John Ellwe, grocer, 40, Niarkt-street, E irlestown, sometime between 10.45 p.m. on M4rch 22ad and 7 a.m, on thP 23:d, and stealing a carving knife., cleaver and steel and about half a pound of twist tobacco, _

Electron Hex ey Duke, manager for Mr Howe, and residing at Myrtle Grove. itsrlestown, said that at 10 45 on the evening of Friday, March 22 ad, he locked up the shop. He left everything safe and sound and holvd the back and front doors. In consequence of i 'formation he received from roe police he visited the shop at 715 a.m. on March 23rd. He entered the front dor in company with bergeant Lines. On going upstairs he found an entrance to the premises had been effected by means of the back win- dow, which hail been brc.ken and the catch drawn back. fhe window was raised. When he left the premises the night before, the window was fastened and unbroken. Further investigations revealed the fact that some bricks bad been removed from over the shop door and the lock I of 'he door had been wrenched off. The drawers in the shop were in a state of great disorder, the contents of some of them haviog been thrown on the 11 'or. The safe had ben tampered with but remained intact. On looking round witness missed the carving knife, steel and cleaver (produced) from the counter, and he also discovered that half a pound of tobacco, made up in two ounce packages, had been taken from a drawer. The total value of the st Alen property was 15s. The prisoner was found in the attic by P.C. Brown and two other men.

Henry Morris, manager of the pawnshop, 42, Market- street, and who resichs on the premises, stated that he was awakened at 6 o'clock 9n the morning of the 23r1 of March by the barking of his dog. He went down- stairs and entered the shop. where he found the prisoner and another man. When they saw him the men ran out of the shop into the pledge office, jumped over the counter, and escaped into the warehouse. Witness pur- sued them and the burglars effected an exit by means of a window. Prisoner ran into the shop of Mr Howe,and the other man escaped. Witness gave information to P.C. Brown. On examining his premises witness Fund the catarmg knife produced on a rack in the warehouse. The cleaver was lying on the safe in the pledge office, and the steel was on the shop counter. He also found a cap and oise or twa candles.

-1" C. Frank Brown stated that he was on duty in Market-street at 6.15 a.m., on the date in question and in conseq eice of what the last witness told him he went to the rear of Mr ilowe's shop and entered the premises by means of a window which was open. He searched the premises and found the prisoner hiding in the attic between the ceiling and the slates. 1:13 arrested the man and took him to the police station where he charged him with breaking and entering Howe's shop and stealing the articles named. Prisoner replied " I am not guilty." Witness searched him and found ia his possession the two packages of tobacco produced. He received the other articles from the witness &Terris. Prisoner, who reserved his defence was committed for trial at the Liverpoel Quarter Sessions. Anderson was then onarg.,rd with breaking and enter- ing the shop of William Jones, 42, Market-street, and stealing 18i in cash, a postal order value 2s, and two silk handkerchiefs value ss.

Henry Morris, manager ot the shop, repeated his evidence in the first CISP, and added that on ex imining his master's premises he found that An entrance had been effected by means of the warehouse window. Two iron bars outside the window had been pulled out of their lead sockets. The window bad been prized open and pushed back. The burglars had got from the ware- house into ne shop by prizing open the door. Witness found the cash drawer in th- pledgeoffice had been privd open and some of the contents spread about the floor. Be missed from the drawer 18g in copper and a postal order for 24. The silk handkerchiefs. which the night previous were sate in the pledge office, had disappeared. The wrapper in which the handkerchiefs were kapt, was found on the floor of the officr4. The windows and doors of the premises were quite secure the previous night. P C. Brown said that when the prisoner was charged with the offmsce he replid, ' I am not guilty," Prisoner was :orninittou for trial on this charge also.

div.head: BETTING PROSECUTIONS. Warn n gton Bookmakers Heavily Fined.
div.p: BETTING PROSECUTIONS. Warn n gton Bookmakers Heavily Fined.
A Policeman Backs Two Winners. The Mayor's Comments.

Several important betting prosecutions occupied the attention of the Warrington magistrates on Monday, and after a prolonged hearing very heavy penalties were inflicted. The magistrates on the Bench were the Mayor (in the chair), Alderman Hutchinson and Heaton, Councillors Smethurst and Pierpoint, and Messrs P Monks, E J Guest; T Birchall, S Wright, and H Tearnton. The first defendant was Annie Mather, 16, Friars'-gate, who was sutntnone I for using the back-yard of her mother's; house in Friars'-lane, for the purpose of batting between February 12* h and March 14th. Mr. A Browne appeared for the defendant and pleaded not guilty. In stetine ton facts for the prosecution, the Chief Constable said there were really two defendants in this case, but Mr Browne eleeted to have them tried separ- ately, although the evidence was identical in each instance He (the Chief Constable) proposed to prove that within the time speei fled the back yard of Mrs *ether's house was need by Miss Mather for the purpose of receiving bets. He weu:d prove that on the 12te of February. the occasion of the Folkestone race meeting. ths card Wal watched by Detective eleaeeek from 12 30 to 1 40, and he saw 28 priming entnr, carrying slips of Paper. Several of them were kniwn to the police. On the same day Police-Constable Mulroy, who was new in that capacity to the defendant effected two te,ts with Miss Mather and her coadjutor is on Method for the Maiden Hipelle Race, and is on Mill Girl for Deal handicap race. The Lin:field Steeplechase inceting was on February 20th, and the place was watched by Meecock and Police-Constable Clough from 12 20 to 1 55. Thirty persons enter- ed, and Malroy again beck eel two hones. Miss Mather seemed to have some misgiving regarding Mutroy on this occasion. Perhaps it was that Mutely was beaming to look more like a poliee.-.an as time went on. (Lauehter) She seemed to be suspicious as to his bona-fidei an I asked her coadjutor, a man named New- ton and another man whether they ought to take bets from him. She suhseqnen'ly decided to do so, and he made two bets. At the same meeting on the !rat day Mulrov backed two more horses. The place was watched between twelve noon end two o'clock, and 63 pereons— on each occasion there were men, women and numerous children—entered the yard. Singu'ar to relate, on this occasion the ooliceman backed two winners. (Laughter.) Fie drew 6 6 Pfrom Miss M then that night. On March 15'11, the Derby Hunt Meting, Meecenk watched the I place from 11.55 to 1 45; and saw 50 persons carrying slips enter the yard The liempton Park meeting was on March 6th, and 30 men, one boy, four women and three girls entered the yard. The police officer saw Miss Mather come out several times and look anxiously lup and down. Altogether twelve bets were made by Mulrov, and a men named Savage on two occs.sions made bets with Miss Mather and the man. Miss Mather appeared to be very much disturbed in her mind about Mulroy. He hod formerly worked at Ohre gas works. She asked a men named Mannion if anyone of the name worke at the gas works. He said there were two there of that name. She ached if " Mic " Melroy was there. He replied that formerly he was hut had joined tile police force. She said "Oh, goodness t And on Saturday he backed two winners with me ia our Yard." (Laughter.) If he (the Chief Constable) proved those facts the magistrates would have little doubt that the yard had been used for the purpose of betting. Detective beeseock said that acting upon instructions he had for some time past been watching the yard of Mrs Mather's house in Friaase-lane. Be made notes of what he saw on each oceasinn. On 'February 12th be watched the hoete from 12 30 to 1.40, and during that time he saw 27 men and one woman enter. Before' entering the yard most of the men palled ont slips of paper and sometimes money. Some stayed in the yard a minute—some less: 0 I February 20th, the Lingli Id Steeplechase meeting, he was with P.C. Clough from 12 30 tn 1 55, and Saw 29 men and one girl enter. On Fenruary 23:d, the Plum oton meeting, he watched the Place from noon to two o'cloCk. Fifty-seven men, two hey., three women and one girl entered. On March sth. the Darby Steeplechase, from 12 5 to 1,45, 40 men, two boys, six women and twe girls went in. OR March 6th, Kenepton Park meetinz,from 12 15; to 1 50,33 men, one boy, four women and three girls entered. He (wit- ness) knew that Mies Mather and another carried on the betting husiness.—Ornes-exernined : Be could not see in the yard. He only saw Miss Mather on toe last date. P.C. Clough corroborated. P.C. Mulrov said he was Instructed to make certain bets at this place. Prior to jnining the police force he was at the gas works. On February 12th, being at that time a policeman, he went to the back yard of Mrs Mather 's house at a quarter past one. He said he wanted to back two horses. Mr Newton said " We don't know you. You are gaits a stranger." He replied " You might as well take from me SS from anyone else." He then backed two horses with Mr Newton. Oa F -Te- rtiary 20th he went again and saw Miss Mather and Mr Newton. He gave Mr Newton a slip ef paper with his name, the narnes of two horses and the money. Re had a shilling on each horse. He saw Mr N ,wton pass the paper and money to Miss Mather. Mies Mather said, "Who are you ? By Jove, I I have been frightened of you all week." Witness repliel " You don't need Co be frightened of me." On February 23rd, Plumpton Steeplechages, he hacked two more horses, Miss Mather Wit 9 there. • Mr Newton took the money. Miss Mather said " Well, Mr Mu'roy—Detective Mulrov." (Laughter). Be did not know whether she made the remark seriously or jokingly He saw Mire; Mather pay money out on that date. He backed two winners and she paid him the money. All together he made eight bets —Crosa-examined : He was Sure 111 Spoke CO Miss Mather in the yard, He made the beta with Mr Newton. When Miss Mather paid the money oat she etood on the yard gate step. The gate we; open. She took the silos in the yard. The Magistrates Clerk (Mr 0 F F White) ruled that the step was part of The yard. John Mannion, !shouter, living on Friars'-green, said! that on February 26-h Miss Mather asked him whether a man named &Wimp worked at the gas works. He told her that two of that name worked there, She asked if " Mtc" NI ulroy was one of them, and he'told her that h was then on the force. She said she was very" feared.. HA had backed tyre winners. Witness told her not to take any more money from him. (Laughter.) James Savage, a corporation labourer, said that on March 13`11 he went to Mather's backyard and made two bets weh Miss Mather. She stood at the gateway. On March 14th he made two more bets. Mr. Browne said he had consulted with his client, who recognized how perfectly hopeless it was in face of the evidence submitted to attempt to make the magistrates believe that she had not used this beck yard for the pur- pose; of betting, and under the circumstances he simply wished to say that what she dii was in the street and not in the yard, and of course in that case she would be liable to a penalty of only £5 and costs under the bee- laws and not the higher penalties under the Bettina Houses Act. She had done nothing except in the street, but the Clerk had over-ruled them upon the purely. technical point as to whether the yard step was in the street or the yard. Mulrov distinctly told them that he never made a bet with Mies Mather except on one occasion He made the bets with Newton. Mills Mather was there but did not speak on several occasions. She assured him (Mr Browne) and wished also to torture the Beach that she did not do any betting, except on the last occasion. She would undertake that the betting would stop, and the yard would not be used for tha purpose again. These were her mother's premises. He asked the magistrates to deal with her as lightly as was consistent with the discharge of their duty. Tne Chief Constable said he had received complaints and had seen Mrs and Miss !leather some time ago. tie knew they were subjected to considerable harassment :e time; gone by—no doubt they deserved it—and he wTihseh - ed them to diecontinne the betting altoeether. gave him an uedertakine that it would be stopped. It was for a short time, but went on again- Mr Browne:--it is only fair to s that that was nearly three years ago: Tne Chief Constable itclinittehat vtehaatotththetemwateosdoiscoHne. would have done anything to tinue the betting, because he did not like prosecuting women. Mr Browne, after consulting with Newton, Said he had advised him that to go into his case would be per- fectly hopeless and a waste of time, and be would there- fore consent to the oases beieg tried together. He, admitted that be had hsd betting traneetions with Mulroy. He only wished to say that the number of persona who entered the yard was far below the number the police had spoken to. The greatest number in a day was ten. Mr Newton had never been summoned before, and was connected with an eld Warrington family. Counciller Pierpeint : We know him well. The Mayor We also know that he has been makine, a living for many years out of this kind of immoral and illegal practice. Mr Newton, who lives at 157, Orford-lane, was sum- moned sit:X*4ly to Mies Mather. The magistrates retired, and on their return into court, The Mayor said : We have very carefully considered these two cases, and have crime to the conclusion, prin.* eipally on account of a sentimental feeling for women, which in cases of this kind 1 perannally do not share in, to tr,..t Miss Mather somewhat diff Tently from Newton Miss Mather will he fined £5O. or an alternative of three months' imprisonment, and Newton will be lined £lOO or an alternative of six months' imprisonment. I should like to say it is a matter of public notoriety that this heuse has been used for many years now for the pur- poses of beving,and I do sincerely hope that the reproach upon the town which ths establishment and mainten• sacs of houses of this kind undoubtedly is will cease, at ny rate as far as this house and family are concerned.
It is not a plelissnt thing for magistrates to adjudicate upon and fine women in oases of this kind. I hope WO wilt never have to delt again. STREET BETTING AND SEIOP .BETTING. HEAVY FINES.

You might ask the witness • whether he was in such prsition as to see everything that wept on ? Mr S:eel (to witness) : Were you in such a position as to see who went into the shop? , P.C. Clough corroborated the last •witness'a evidence. —By Mr Sued : You could not see what took place inside the shop ?—Witness : N. Mr Steel, on behalf of the clef eodant, submitt-d that the police had failed to prove the charge nosde against the defendant ot I.lBloe the shop for the purpose of h•tte- log. It was not a betting house within the terms of the Act of 1853.

The Chief Constable olinted Out that the defendant was not charged with keeping a betting house. Mr. Steel quoted a case showing that it was necessarir to prove that the place was used by the detendan; exclusively tor his own purpose. This shop was not the defendant's, but belonged to a mai named Lavin, and he submitted that it was not being' used for betting within the terms of the act of 1853. It had not blot provel by the p Ace that tois NVI3 a shop where a beget' fide betting business was carried on. If the defendant went there and made a casual loft that was not a using of the premises for the purpose of betting within the terms of the Act. This shop was surely not going to Do termed a betting house. The Chief Constable : I submit we have'nt to proo any exclusive right of using the premises for betting. tidr Steel : The obj,nt of the act was the suppression of betting-houses. fie submitted it had not besn proved, and did not come within the terms of the SA. tin g Ant of .1853. _ _ . _

The Chief Constable contended that it did apply. The Mayor said Mr Steel's remarks would have bees pertinent if the prosecution had been taken under the Gaming Houses act of 1854, but the case was applicable to the betting act of 1853

Mr Steel :I contend that the defendant is not in occupation of the premises. The Mayor : If the police have not snffieient evidence to prove that he is the occupier it dons not follow that they have not sufficient evidence to prove that be made use of the premises for betting purposes. We have the evidence of the witness S avage that the dnfendant used this place for the purpose of making bits. Yen have no diriputed anything up to the cresent. Mr Steel: I don't inte id to dispute, but I contend that before the defendant can be a user, it must he' habitual occupation.

The Mayor: No, the act does not say so. Mr Steel: There is a case decided where a man went three clays in succession and the court held that it wall not habitual. He contended that this was not habitual use for the purpose of betting. Continuing, be se,/d if the court was against him on that point he would sok thorn to be as lenient as they possibly could. This mao had resorted to this way of !risking a livelihood on the persuasion of friends. He was not a bookmaker but acted,for somebody else. He had no money and did not belong to any club. Any fines inflicced would have to come out of the derAndant's own pocket. div.p: OUR NEW SERIAL. OUR NEW SERIAL. We have pleasure in announcing that we have secured for publication in our columns a thrilling btory entitled. "THE LADDER OF GUILT," BY ULYSS R.IGERS, fiuttcr of "Mime," •' For Love and the Queen," "Wedded in Mystery," etc. ---_--- Mr. ULYS9 ROGERS, the author of our new story, contrary to the experience of most young authors, confesses to having met with a very kindly reception upon coming to London and placing his literary wares at the disposal 0 London editors. He ascribes this success to the fact that as a provincial journalist he took years endeavouring to stud./ the exact requirements of the story-reading public before venturing to exhibit his productions for editorial criticisms. Mr. Timers &nine the three years he has devoted himseli to fiction has published several serial stories and some scores of short ones, contri- buting to practically all the popular London Magazines d weekly veriodicals. " Mime." "For Love and Queen," and Wended in Mystery." have gained Mr Rogers a reputation which will, Without doubt, be considerably enhanced by his latest serial, "THE LADDER OF QUILT." "THE LADDER OF GUILT." "THE LAnnizu OF GUILT" plunges the reader into the thick of the plot from the very commence- ment, and the Interest is maintained through every initalment. It is a story of love, of bate, and of the descending steps in 'the ladder of guilt" to which a weak- minded man is led when once the balance of his life goes wrong owing to an unrequited affection. It is a story of country life and, also, to a great extent deals with prison experiences and systems. A Particularly sensational Chapter is that in which the last penalty of the law is evaded in what might almost be regarded as a miraculous manner, were it not that fiction, in this case, as in most others, has a wonderful counterpart in fact. To say more regarding this extraordinary passage would be but to spoil the reader's appetite and spoil the effect of the scene. "T lIE LADDER OF GUILT." The opening chapters of this exciting Story will appear in our columns on. APRIL 12m. APRIL 12m. APRIL 12m.
